rationale: PD-1 blockade (budigalimab) and anti-α4β7 (ABBV-382) for post-ATI viral control are both mechanistically plausible, but historical ATI trials of immunotherapies mostly fail, and phase 1b budigalimab data showed only a minority of participants with delayed rebound. Placebo viral control at week 24 (<1000 copies/mL without ART restart) should be near 0–5%, so a strong signal in one arm could reach significance. With only ~23 participants per arm, an arm would need roughly 30% or more controllers. Multiple active arms help a little, but the endpoint may also be analyzed only descriptively, which lowers the chance of a formally significant result.

This is a non-inferiority bridging study in China comparing two devices that deliver the same BDP/formoterol formulation. A similar design already succeeded in Europe (Foster NEXThaler vs pMDI on morning PEF), and both drugs are well established, so the device switch is unlikely to change efficacy. Patients have well-controlled asthma after a pMDI run-in, so morning PEF should stay stable in both arms, and with about 494 patients and a typical margin of around -15 L/min, non-inferiority is very likely. The main risks are handling problems with the DPI or higher variance in a Chinese population, which are modest concerns.

Orforglipron is an oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist that produced large placebo-adjusted weight loss in Phase 2 (about 9–15% in obesity, and meaningful loss in T2D). Here it is tested against placebo in about 1,600 patients over 72 weeks, so the trial has enormous power for percent weight change. Even in T2D, where weight loss is smaller, a placebo-adjusted difference of several percent is near-certain to be highly significant. I recall that Lilly reported ATTAIN-2 in 2025 as meeting its primary endpoint, with about 10.5% weight loss on the highest dose versus about 2.2% on placebo.

This is a pragmatic, unblinded PCORI-funded SMART trial testing lactulose and then virtual Tai-Chi against enhanced usual care for a hierarchical composite of falls, overt HE, transplant and death over 24 weeks. With about 233 participants split across factorial and sequential comparisons, power to detect a moderate reduction in a composite event rate is limited. Evidence that lactulose or Tai-Chi prevents falls in cirrhosis rests mostly on small or observational studies, and the enhanced usual care control (protein and fall-prevention counseling) narrows any between-arm difference. Pragmatic behavioral and repurposed-drug trials on hard clinical composites have a low base rate of success, so I put the chance of a significant primary result at roughly 15%.

Prehospital trauma resuscitation trials with a 30-day mortality primary endpoint seldom reach significance. PAMPer is the notable exception, while RePHILL was negative, and 1,020 patients can only detect a fairly large absolute mortality reduction. The comparator partly includes crystalloid-only care, which could widen the treatment difference, and observational data favoring whole blood plus experienced investigators (the Sperry/PAMPer group) make success plausible. Still, dilution from patients who are not actually bleeding, the small volume (up to two units), and open-label pragmatic conduct argue for a probability below even.

This is a small (58 enrolled, likely fewer evaluable after induction failures), single-site pilot comparing a combination topical nucleoside cream against an active comparator, docosanol, rather than placebo. Topical acyclovir and penciclovir have historically shown only modest benefits in herpes labialis, and aborting vesicle formation is a hard endpoint with small expected differences between active treatments. With a binary outcome and roughly 20–25 evaluable subjects per arm, the trial is badly underpowered for anything short of a very large effect, so statistical significance is unlikely even if the cream works somewhat better.

I recall that Pfizer announced in 2025 that HER2CLIMB-05 met its primary PFS endpoint, but this estimate is what I would have given before the readout. Tucatinib's activity on top of trastuzumab is established from HER2CLIMB, and PATINA showed that intensifying HP maintenance (with palbociclib) can meaningfully extend PFS. The endpoint is investigator-assessed PFS against placebo plus HP, in a large trial (n=654) with a long-PFS population, which makes a modest hazard ratio detectable. Risks include toxicity-driven discontinuation of tucatinib and a diluted effect in patients already responding to induction, so a moderately favourable probability is warranted.

OpSCF is an anti-stem cell factor antibody that targets the mast-cell SCF/KIT axis, a mechanism without validated efficacy in atopic dermatitis. Early-phase dermatology trials of novel mechanisms succeed at modest rates. With about 50 patients, a 14-week course, and placebo EASI responses typically around 30–40%, the study is only powered for a large effect, and the 90% CIs in the secondary outcomes point to an exploratory, signal-seeking design. I believe Insmed later reported the study failed to show meaningful efficacy and dropped the program, but my pre-readout estimate would have been low on these grounds alone.

The first primary endpoint compares combined pre- and post-contrast gadoquatrane MRI against unenhanced MRI on blinded reader scores for contrast enhancement. Contrast agents almost always win this comparison by a wide margin, and 410 patients gives ample power. Gadoquatrane's high relaxivity means 0.04 mmol Gd/kg should still give strong enhancement, and Phase 2 data supported the dose. I recall Bayer announcing that the QUANTI pivotal studies met their primary endpoints, but even without that, my prior forecast would have been very high.

Phase 2 Alzheimer's trials of novel symptomatic or disease-modifying oral agents rarely beat placebo on ADAS-Cog13 over 26 weeks, and the base rate is well under 15%. AR1001 (mirodenafil, a PDE5 inhibitor) has only preclinical support for this indication, and 210 patients across three arms is underpowered for the small effects plausible in this setting. I recall that AriBio's topline reported no statistically significant difference on the primary endpoints in the overall population, with benefit claimed only in post-hoc subgroups, though I would have forecast a low probability regardless.

This is PIONEER TEENS, a placebo-controlled phase 3 trial of oral semaglutide on HbA1c, a sensitive endpoint. Every GLP-1 receptor agonist tested this way in pediatric type 2 diabetes has beaten placebo: liraglutide (ELLIPSE), dulaglutide (AWARD-PEDS) and exenatide QW. With 132 participants and a likely placebo-adjusted HbA1c difference of about 1%, the trial should have high power. The main risks are poor adherence to the strict fasting dosing rules in teenagers and a high placebo or rescue response. I vaguely recall it reported a significant HbA1c reduction, but my forecast rests mainly on the strong prior.

This is ODYSSEY-HCM. I recall BMS announcing in 2025 that it missed both dual primary endpoints, KCCQ-CSS and pVO2, but the forecast below is made as of before the readout. The prior evidence was weak: the phase 2 MAVERICK-HCM trial in non-obstructive HCM showed NT-proBNP reductions but no clear benefit on symptoms or function. Without an outflow gradient to relieve, the mechanism that drove EXPLORER-HCM's success in obstructive HCM is absent, and lowering contractility could even hurt some patients. A large, well-powered trial, a KCCQ endpoint prone to placebo response, and only one of two primary endpoints needing to succeed give some upside, so I put the pre-readout chance at about 30%.

AD109 (aroxybutynin/atomoxetine) had supportive Phase 2 data (MARIPOSA and earlier crossover studies) showing clinically meaningful AHI reductions versus placebo, and the mechanism of restoring upper-airway dilator muscle tone has a solid physiological rationale. AHI change measured by PSG is an objective endpoint with low placebo response, and n=660 gives ample power for the effect sizes seen in Phase 2. The main risks are attrition or tolerability over a one-year study diluting the 6-month effect. I recall that Apnimed announced LunAIRo met its primary endpoint, but before the readout I would have estimated roughly 80%.

Before the readout, the evidence already argued against a large effect. PRODEX found dexmedetomidine non-inferior to propofol but not faster to extubation, and SPICE III and MENDS2 showed no meaningful advantage over usual sedation. The design is pragmatic and open-label, with propofol allowed as a top-up in the alpha-2 arms, which dilutes any between-arm difference, and the base rate for ICU sedation trials beating an active comparator on duration endpoints is low. I recall the published result: neither dexmedetomidine nor clonidine significantly shortened time to extubation versus propofol.

Ripasudil, a ROCK inhibitor, has mechanistic support and small Japanese studies suggesting it reduces endothelial cell loss after cataract surgery and promotes endothelial recovery. However, ECD measured by specular microscopy is noisy, the post-cataract surgery population likely has heterogeneous endothelial status, and with about 165 patients per pooled arm a modest treatment effect may not reach significance. I vaguely recall Kowa scaling back the K-321 program in the US, which tempers my optimism, so I put this somewhat below the typical phase 3 base rate.

This is a small (about 84 patients), open-label, single-center NHLBI phase 2 trial testing whether a 12-week sirolimus course prevents aplastic anemia relapse after cyclosporine withdrawal. The rationale rests mainly on mouse models of immune tolerance, with no human efficacy data. Expected control relapse rates are about 30-40%, and many enrollees will be long-term cyclosporine responders who may relapse less often, so power to detect anything short of a large effect from a brief course is limited. Academic phase 2 trials of repurposed immunomodulators often miss their primary endpoint, so I put the chance of a significant reduction in 2-year relapse at about 18%.

The primary comparison is in Cohort A1: vibostolimab plus pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab alone on BICR-assessed ORR in PD-L1-positive cervical cancer, a randomized phase 2 arm that is probably modestly sized. Anti-TIGIT add-ons to PD-1 blockade have repeatedly failed to show meaningful benefit, including tiragolumab in the SKYSCRAPER trials and vibostolimab's own KEYVIBE program, which Merck largely discontinued. Pembrolizumab alone already gives a reasonable response rate in cervical cancer, so a statistically significant ORR gain in a phase 2-sized randomization is unlikely. I don't specifically recall this cohort's result, but the class evidence points strongly toward a negative outcome.

AZD2693 (ION839) is a PNPLA3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide. Early data showed liver-fat reduction in 148M carriers, and the human genetics behind the target are strong, but histologic NASH resolution at 52 weeks has not yet been shown for this mechanism. Phase 2b NASH trials hit the resolution endpoint only for agents with strong metabolic or anti-inflammatory effects (GLP-1s, FGF21s, resmetirom). With about 73 patients per arm, likely including heterozygous carriers who may respond less, and placebo resolution rates of 10–20%, the trial needs a sizeable effect, so success is plausible but uncertain.

BPL-003 is intranasal 5-MeO-DMT, and this design mirrors COMP360's positive Phase 2b: high dose vs a near-inactive 0.3 mg 'active placebo' in TRD, with psychological support and MADRS as the endpoint. Psychedelic trials against low-dose comparators tend to show large effect sizes, partly because functional unblinding is hard to avoid. That makes a significant Day 29 difference with about 65 patients per arm fairly likely, though single-dose durability to 4 weeks is a real risk. I recall Beckley/atai announcing in 2025 that the 12 mg dose met the primary endpoint, but my pre-readout estimate would have been about 0.65–0.7.

Levo's earlier Phase 3 CARE-PWS trial missed its primary endpoint, and the 3.2 mg TID dose being tested here only looked good on post hoc or secondary analyses. That makes this a confirmatory bet on a subgroup signal. PWS hyperphagia trials have a poor history, with caregiver-rated HQ-CT endpoints showing large placebo responses, and about 175 participants gives limited power for the modest effect expected. I recall that Acadia announced COMPASS PWS did not meet its primary endpoint, but my pre-readout estimate, based on the base rate and the prior data, would have been roughly one in three.

Benralizumab already failed its primary endpoints in COPD in GALATHEA and TERRANOVA. Those post-hoc analyses pointed to benefit in patients with higher eosinophils and frequent exacerbations, which is the population RESOLUTE enriched for (≥300/μL, on triple therapy). Mepolizumab's MATINEE and dupilumab's BOREAS/NOTUS trials support the type-2 mechanism in eosinophilic COPD, but enrollment was cut to 689 and the first primary analysis uses only the ≥3-exacerbation subgroup, which reduces power. I recall that AstraZeneca reported RESOLUTE did not meet its primary endpoint; my prior estimate would have been slightly below even odds.

Gastroparesis symptom trials have a poor track record because placebo response is high and patient-reported nausea endpoints are noisy; relamorelin and several other agents failed in phase 3 despite promising phase 2 data. Tradipitant's positive phase 2 nausea result offers some mechanistic support, but NK-1 antagonism has not been validated in chronic gastroparesis, and phase 3 replication of a single phase 2 PRO signal often fails. I recall that this trial missed its primary endpoint in the ITT population, and Vanda attributed the miss to rescue medication and inadequate drug exposure. Before the readout I would have estimated about one-third.

This is ECHELON-3, and I recall that it met its OS primary endpoint (HR about 0.63), which led to FDA approval in early 2025; the estimate below is what I would have given beforehand. Before readout, the case rested on encouraging phase 1/2 BV+R2 data (ORR around 57%, including CD30-negative patients) and the large effect sizes plausible in a heavily pretreated, transplant/CAR-T-ineligible population with short survival. Against that, OS as the primary endpoint in a 240-patient trial is demanding, since later-line therapies like bispecifics could dilute the benefit. Add-on ADC trials in DLBCL also have a mixed track record, which tempered the pre-readout estimate to a little under even odds.

Pediatric migraine prevention trials have a poor record because placebo response is high, as in CHAMP and the adolescent chronic-migraine topiramate study, and the chronic-migraine population makes this worse. CGRP antibodies work in adults, and fremanezumab later showed modest benefit in pediatric episodic migraine, so the mechanism has some support in this age group. The mid-study protocol amendments and the adolescent-only primary analysis add uncertainty, and 284 participants split across three arms leaves limited power for a small effect over a large placebo response. I believe OASIS-CM was reported as not meeting its primary endpoint, but my pre-readout estimate would have been about one in three.

Randomized-withdrawal designs in sleep disorders usually succeed, as Xywav's IH withdrawal study did, and pitolisant has proven wake-promoting efficacy in narcolepsy, so the prior leans favorable. Against that, pitolisant's ESS effect sizes are modest, the 4-week withdrawal window is short, and placebo patients may not lose benefit quickly, all of which limit separation with about 64 patients per arm. I recall Harmony reporting that INTUNE missed statistical significance on the ESS primary endpoint because the placebo arm held its improvement. My pre-readout estimate is still roughly 55–60%.

TAK-861 (oveporexton), an orexin 2 receptor agonist, gave very large MWT improvements in the phase 2b NT1 trial (NEJM 2025), with mean sleep latency gains of roughly 20+ minutes over placebo, so effect sizes are huge relative to a 168-patient, three-arm Phase 3 replication. The mechanism directly replaces the missing orexin signaling in NT1, and the primary endpoint is objective MWT against placebo. I recall Takeda announcing in July 2025 that both Phase 3 trials (FirstLight and RadiantLight) met all primary and secondary endpoints, which fits this prior. The remaining risk is mainly operational.

This is a very small (n=11) single-site crossover trial of nitrate-rich versus nitrate-depleted beetroot juice, with peak treadmill time as the primary endpoint. Earlier acute studies (e.g., Kenjale 2011) suggested modest walking benefits in PAD. Later and larger studies of nitrate supplementation in PAD and HFpEF have often been null, and treadmill time is highly variable. Given limited power and an uncertain effect size, the chance of a significant result is low, though crossover designs reduce variance somewhat.

Earlier Phase 3 trials of intra-articular lorecivivint (OA-11, OA-10) missed their 12-week pain NRS primary endpoints, and mechanistic support came mainly from post-hoc subgroup and structural signals. Knee OA pain trials with intra-articular saline or vehicle controls have large placebo responses, which makes a modest single-injection effect hard to detect, even with about 250 patients per arm. This trial appears redesigned around earlier subgroup learnings, but Biosplice has a repeated record of missing primary endpoints. I don't specifically recall this trial's outcome, so I keep the probability below the typical Phase 3 base rate.

Povorcitinib, an oral JAK1 inhibitor, showed a clear dose-dependent HiSCR50 benefit over placebo at week 12 in a Phase 2 HS trial, and JAK inhibition has shown activity in HS with upadacitinib. With about 206 patients per arm, two active doses, and the standard HiSCR50 endpoint, the trial is well powered even if the placebo response is high (around 30%), which is the main risk in HS trials. I recall Incyte announcing that both STOP-HS Phase 3 trials met the HiSCR50 primary endpoint at both doses, but before the readout I would have estimated about 0.85.

Phase 2 trials in dementia rarely succeed, and a 16-week trial with ~160 patients has limited power to detect a CDR-SB difference in DLB, even though the earlier phase 2a AscenD-LB trial showed some post-hoc signals for neflamapimod. Selecting patients with plasma ptau181 to enrich for pure DLB is a sensible design choice, but the mechanism is unvalidated and the prior evidence is weak. I recall that topline results reported the primary CDR-SB endpoint was not met, which the sponsor attributed to a new capsule formulation producing lower drug exposure. Ignoring that recollection, a pre-readout estimate of about 25% reflects a modestly above-base-rate prior.

SM04554 is Samumed's (now Biosplice's) topical Wnt-pathway modulator. Its earlier Phase 2 US trials gave mixed signals, with inconsistent dose-response and modest or non-significant hair-count differences versus vehicle, so mechanistic support is weak. Novel topical hair-growth agents rarely beat vehicle robustly in large trials, and this study ran only in Turkey, which points to a regional registration strategy rather than strong confidence. The 675 subjects give adequate power for a moderate effect, but the prior evidence suggests any true effect is small, so I put the chance of a significant win on 48-week non-vellus hair count at roughly 20%.

This is FINE-ONE, which uses a surrogate UACR endpoint, and I recall it was reported positive, with roughly a 25% placebo-adjusted UACR reduction. Even setting that aside, finerenone reliably lowers UACR by about 30% in type 2 diabetic CKD (FIDELIO, ARTS-DN), and the albuminuria-lowering mechanism should carry over to type 1 diabetes. With 242 participants, background ACEi/ARB, no SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA use, and an endpoint averaged over months 3 and 6, power to detect a 25–30% reduction is high. The main risks are variability in UACR and dose down-titration in lower-eGFR participants, which are modest.

This is the VERIFY Phase 3 trial of rusfertide. The Phase 2 REVIVE randomized withdrawal study already showed a large effect, with about 60% vs 17% responders on rusfertide vs placebo. Hepcidin mimetics have a strong mechanistic rationale for controlling erythrocytosis, and against placebo in phlebotomy-dependent patients the responder endpoint should separate by a wide margin; with about 293 patients, power is very high. I recall that VERIFY met its primary endpoint (about 77% vs 33%, p<0.0001), but even before the readout a probability of roughly 0.9 or higher was warranted.

Pharmacotherapy trials for cannabis use disorder almost always fail, and guanfacine has only lab-study evidence (modest effects on withdrawal and relapse) behind it, so the base rate here is low. The trial was cut short by a federally mandated research pause, leaving 22 participants, which gives very little power for a noisy EMA-based use outcome. Its stated aims are exploratory and feasibility-focused, which further lowers the chance of a significant primary result. A chance finding is possible but unlikely.

This is the zunsemetinib (ATI-450) Phase 2b RA trial, and I recall that in November 2023 Aclaris announced it did not meet its primary endpoint (ACR20 at week 12), after which the program was discontinued. Setting that aside, the prior was poor: p38 MAPK inhibitors have repeatedly failed in RA because of transient efficacy and tachyphylaxis, and MK2 inhibition sits downstream on the same pathway. The Phase 2a data were small and open-label, and Eastern European placebo response rates are high, so a modest effect with about 80 patients per arm was at real risk. A pre-readout forecast would have sat around 25–30%, but I am giving a lower figure because I recall the failure.

Teprotumumab already showed that IGF-1R inhibition works in chronic, low-activity TED, with a 62% vs 16% proptosis response in its placebo-controlled chronic-TED trial. Veligrotug had shown strong proptosis responses in Phase 1/2 and in THRIVE (active TED). With about 188 participants and a large expected effect over a low placebo responder rate, the trial is well powered, though chronic disease carries some risk of a smaller effect. I recall that THRIVE-2 reported meeting its primary endpoint (about 56% vs 8%, p<0.0001), but my pre-readout estimate would have been roughly 0.9.

Covalent BTK inhibitors have consistently beaten bendamustine-rituximab on PFS in untreated CLL (ibrutinib in ALLIANCE A041202, zanubrutinib in SEQUOIA, with similar BTKi-based results in ELEVATE-TN). Pirtobrutinib already had strong single-arm activity in BRUIN. With 282 patients, IRC-assessed PFS, and an expected hazard ratio around 0.3–0.4, the trial is well powered; the main risk would be immature events, which is unlikely given the 40-month window. I recall Lilly announcing that BRUIN CLL-313 met its PFS primary endpoint, but the pre-readout estimate on mechanism and class evidence alone would still be about 0.93.

This is NRG BN001, which tests hypofractionated dose escalation (75 Gy in 30 fractions via IMRT or protons) with temozolomide against the standard 60 Gy for glioblastoma. Radiation dose escalation beyond 60 Gy has repeatedly failed to improve survival in glioblastoma, for example in RTOG 98-03 and in other boost trials, and most interventions added in newly diagnosed GBM fail on overall survival. I recall that BN001 found no overall survival benefit in either group, but setting that aside, the prior is low given the weak mechanistic and historical support. A randomized phase II with a lenient one-sided alpha could still show a nominal benefit by chance, which keeps the probability slightly above the floor.

This small Phase 2a trial (about 18 per arm) tests whether adding OCA 5 mg to bezafibrate lowers ALP more than bezafibrate alone at 12 weeks. Both mechanisms are validated in PBC and their effects on ALP should be additive, so the low-dose comparison (OCA + BZF 100 mg vs BZF 100 mg) has a good chance of significance, since OCA alone typically lowers ALP by roughly 20–30%. The high-dose comparison is harder because BZF 400 mg alone already produces large ALP reductions, and small arms limit power for either comparison. I vaguely recall Intercept describing the combination data positively but not whether the formal comparison was significant, so I put this moderately above the Phase 2 base rate.

The record itself shows the trial was stopped early on DSMB recommendation, with conditional power of 0.54% for the primary outcome and a trend toward more unfavorable outcomes in the BCZD arm. Enrollment reached only 94 of the planned 156 participants, which further reduces the chance of a significant superiority result on time to culture conversion. Bedaquiline-based regimens do have biological plausibility for faster sterilization, but the interim data clearly pointed against success. I do not recall the published result, so I am forecasting from this record alone.

This appears to be Apnimed's MARIPOSA Phase 2b dose-finding trial, and I recall topline results reporting a statistically significant reduction in AHI for AD109 versus placebo. Setting that aside, the prior is still strong. Earlier single-night and crossover studies of atomoxetine plus oxybutynin showed large AHI reductions, and AHI is an objective PSG endpoint. The primary analysis pools both AD109 arms against placebo with roughly 70+ patients per group, giving ample power for the plausible effect size; the main risks are a smaller effect with chronic dosing and variability in night-to-night AHI.

This is a small (n=114), investigator-initiated, open-label non-inferiority trial comparing low-dose periurethral estradiol with standard intravaginal application for preventing recurrent UTI. Periurethral application is biologically plausible and many clinicians already use it, so a large true difference is unlikely. However, with roughly 57 per arm and a binary 6-month UTI-free outcome, the confidence interval for the difference will be wide (±18 percentage points or so), so meeting any reasonable margin is uncertain even if the techniques are truly similar. Attrition and the halved dose make imprecision a real risk, so I put the chance of formally establishing non-inferiority slightly below even.

This is BaxHTN, a large Phase 3 trial of an aldosterone synthase inhibitor whose mechanism is well supported: BrigHTN showed a placebo-adjusted SBP reduction of about 11 mmHg, and HALO's miss in a milder population was partly attributed to conduct issues. With roughly 260 patients per arm, a diuretic-treated uncontrolled/resistant population, and spironolactone-like efficacy expected, power to detect a 5–8 mmHg placebo-adjusted difference is very high. I recall BaxHTN being reported positive at ESC 2025, with placebo-adjusted reductions of about 9–10 mmHg for both doses, though my forecast rests mainly on the prior evidence and design.

Phase 3 IPF trials have a poor track record (pamrevlumab, ziritaxestat and others failed), which argues for a modest prior. The main supporting evidence is a post hoc analysis of the INCREASE trial in PH-ILD, where inhaled treprostinil improved FVC with the clearest signal in the IPF subgroup, plus a plausible antifibrotic rationale. With about 600 patients over 52 weeks, the trial is well powered for an FVC effect of 80–100 mL if the effect is real, but post hoc signals often fail to replicate. I recall that TETON-2 was announced as positive on FVC, but beforehand I would have put it near a coin flip.

Adding lenvatinib to pembrolizumab has repeatedly failed in phase 3 (LEAP-002, -003, -006, -007, -008, -010, -011), and Merck discontinued LEAP-014 and LEAP-015 in 2024 after futility or lack of benefit in related trials. The record says close-out activities began under Amendment 09 with no safety reasons given, which points to futility or a strategic stop. The control arm, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, is an active comparator that is hard to beat on overall survival. I recall that Merck announced LEAP-014 did not improve OS, so even a pre-readout estimate would be low given the program-wide failures.

Inclusion body myositis has a long record of failed randomized trials, including bimagrumab, arimoclomol and immunosuppressants, and the IBMFRS declines slowly, so a 76-week change-from-baseline comparison is hard to win. ABC008 (ulviprubart, anti-KLRG1 depletion of cytotoxic T cells) has a plausible mechanism, with phase 1 data showing target-cell depletion but no controlled efficacy evidence. About 67 patients per arm gives modest power against a small expected effect, though two doses offer two chances. I have no confident recollection of the topline result, so I stay near the low base rate for IBM.

IGF-1R inhibition is strongly validated in active TED: teprotumumab produced roughly 70-80% proptosis responders versus about 10-20% on placebo. With about 30 patients per arm, even a substantially weaker oral small-molecule effect could reach significance. The main risks are whether oral linsitinib achieves enough orbital target engagement and the small sample, though success in either dose arm counts. I recall Sling reporting that the high dose met the primary proptosis endpoint, but my pre-readout estimate, weighing mechanism validation against small-molecule uncertainty, is about 0.6.

IL-6 receptor blockade has mechanistic and clinical support in TED: a small randomized trial of tocilizumab in steroid-resistant disease reported improvements in activity and proptosis. The primary endpoint, a ≥2 mm proptosis responder rate in active TED versus placebo, has a low placebo response rate, which helps, although IL-6 blockade's effect on proptosis is likely smaller than IGF-1R inhibitors'. The main risks are the modest sample (127 total, with the active-TED subgroup smaller still) and a possibly modest effect size. Roche running a twin phase 3 program signals reasonable confidence, so I place the probability somewhat above the phase 3 base rate.

In Phase 2, enlicitide (MK-0616) lowered LDL-C by roughly 41–61% versus placebo, so this nearly 2,900-patient placebo-controlled Phase 3 has overwhelming power for a percent-change LDL-C endpoint. PCSK9 inhibition is a fully validated mechanism, and the biomarker endpoint makes success very likely. Merck announced in 2025 that CORALreef Lipids met its primary endpoint, with about a 55–60% placebo-adjusted LDL-C reduction at week 24. Judged only on pre-readout information, the probability would still have been about 0.98–0.99.

The primary endpoint compares two active danazol doses (400 vs 200 mg/day) on the proportion of patients with ≥50% reduction in telomere attrition at 6 months, in a small (n=18) open-label single-site crossover trial. Danazol has prior evidence of slowing telomere attrition at 800 mg. A significant difference between two lower doses, both expected to be active, is unlikely with this sample size and a noisy 6-month telomere measurement. NIH-run trials like this often report descriptively without a powered between-dose test, so a clear statistically significant win for one arm is improbable.

The first-listed primary endpoint compares combined pre- and post-gadoquatrane MRI against unenhanced MRI on lesion visualization (contrast enhancement). For any gadolinium agent, including one given at a reduced 0.04 mmol/kg dose, superiority over unenhanced images is almost guaranteed, and phase 2 data showed gadoquatrane's high relaxivity. Contrast-agent phase 3 trials with this design succeed nearly every time, and I recall Bayer announcing that the QUANTI CNS study met its primary endpoints. The forecast I would have made before the readout is still very high.

Tralokinumab, an IL-13 antibody, is approved for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, and IL-4/IL-13 blockade with dupilumab clearly beat placebo on IGA 0/1 in atopic hand and foot dermatitis (about 40% vs 17%). Tralokinumab's effect in whole-body AD is more modest, but a placebo-controlled trial of about 235 patients on IGA-AHE 0/1 at week 16 should have adequate power for a plausible 15–20 point difference. I vaguely recall LEO announcing that the ADHAND trial met its primary endpoint, though I am not certain. Before the readout I would still have put the probability around 0.8.

Phase 3 disease-modification trials in neurodegenerative dementias have very low success rates. This one enrolled only about 119 patients with a slowly progressing, heterogeneous FTD-GRN population, which gives little power to detect a slowing of CDR plus NACC FTLD-SB over 96 weeks. The mechanism (sortilin blockade raising progranulin) has strong biomarker support but no proven clinical efficacy. I recall that Alector reported the plasma progranulin co-primary was met but the clinical CDR plus NACC FTLD-SB endpoint was not, so I would have forecast about 15% beforehand.

Before readout, the evidence for asundexian was mixed. PACIFIC-STROKE missed its covert-infarct endpoint, though an exploratory signal in atherosclerotic patients motivated this enriched population, and OCEANIC-AF was stopped early because asundexian was inferior to apixaban, raising doubts about the 50 mg dose's potency. Against that, the trial is very large and event-driven (n≈12,300) and the comparator is placebo on top of antiplatelets, so a moderate true effect would likely be detected; I would have put success at roughly 35-40%. I recall that Bayer announced in late 2025 that OCEANIC-STROKE met its primary efficacy endpoint without increasing major bleeding, but this forecast reflects the pre-readout estimate.

Rimegepant every-other-day dosing already met this same primary endpoint (change in monthly migraine days) in the pivotal global prevention trial, with a modest effect of about 0.8 days versus placebo (p≈0.01) in roughly 700 patients. An Asia/China acute-treatment trial was also positive, supporting efficacy in this population. With 787 participants, power to detect a similar effect is about 80–90%. The main risks are the small effect size and a possibly high placebo response in Chinese sites, so I set the probability somewhat below what the power calculation alone would suggest.

Pediatric acute migraine trials have a poor track record: high placebo response has sunk many triptan studies, and only a few, such as rizatriptan with an enrichment design, have succeeded. Lasmiditan has robust adult efficacy, roughly a 10–12 point gain in 2-hour pain freedom over placebo, and a large Stage 1 sample (~800) gives decent power if even a modest effect carries over to children. Against that, the primary likely rests on the unenriched Stage 1 comparison with weight-based moderate doses, where placebo response in children 6–17 can be 25–35%. Balancing the strong adult mechanism data against the pediatric failure base rate, I put the chance of success somewhat below even.

This is IMvigor011. I recall that Roche announced in 2025 that it met its primary DFS endpoint, with an OS benefit as well, presented at ESMO 2025. Before the readout, the case rested on the exploratory ctDNA-positive subgroup of IMvigor010: that trial failed overall, but atezolizumab showed clear DFS and OS benefit in ctDNA-positive patients (HR about 0.58), and CheckMate 274 had validated adjuvant PD-1 blockade in MIBC. The ctDNA-positive population has a high event rate, which gives good power against placebo, but the hypothesis came from a post-hoc subgroup of a failed trial, so a moderately favorable prior of about two-thirds was justified.

This is Janssen's AFFINITY trial, and I recall that it did not show a statistically significant MDA benefit for the combination over guselkumab monotherapy. Before the readout, I would still have been skeptical. The comparator is an active, effective IL-23 inhibitor, and the population is TNF-inadequate responders, who may respond poorly to adding another TNF blocker. With about 45 patients per arm, only a large difference in MDA rates (roughly 20 or more percentage points) would reach significance. The VEGA combination signal in ulcerative colitis gave some mechanistic support, but a Phase 2a trial this small against an active control warrants a below-base-rate estimate of about 25–30%.

Lerodalcibep is a PCSK9-binding adnectin. Phase 2 showed LDL-C reductions of roughly 60–70%, and PCSK9 inhibition in HeFH reliably produces large, highly significant placebo-adjusted LDL-C reductions. With 478 patients randomized 2:1 against placebo, the trial has overwhelming power on percent change in LDL-C, so only an operational or assay failure could cause a miss. I recall that LIBerate-HeFH reported about a 59% placebo-adjusted LDL-C reduction at week 24 (p<0.0001).

Garetosmab, an anti-activin A antibody, targets the central mechanism of FOP. In the Phase 2 LUMINA-1 trial it reduced new heterotopic ossification lesions by about 90% versus placebo, even though that trial's primary endpoint, total lesion volume, was not met. Choosing new-lesion count as the Phase 3 primary endpoint plays directly to that strong prior signal, and a large effect could reach significance even with about 63 patients across two doses. I recall Regeneron announcing that OPTIMA met its primary endpoint with roughly 90% or greater lesion reduction, but before the readout I would still have put this high given the mechanistic and Phase 2 evidence.

Lanifibranor is a pan-PPAR agonist with a pioglitazone-like insulin-sensitizing mechanism. It already lowered HbA1c in the NATIVE phase 2b, so an absolute reduction of about 1% versus placebo in T2DM patients with baseline HbA1c of 7–10% is plausible. Even with only 39 enrolled (roughly 13 per arm, after early termination), an effect that large against a typical SD of about 0.9% gives reasonable power, and adding empagliflozin should widen the gap further. I recall the LEGEND topline reporting significant HbA1c reductions for both arms, but beforehand I would have put this around 0.75–0.8 because of the small sample.

Azithromycin is highly active against V. cholerae and is a first-line single-dose treatment, and earlier household-contact studies of tetracycline/doxycycline chemoprophylaxis showed fewer secondary infections, so the mechanism is well supported. Household contacts in Dhaka acquire infection at substantial rates in the first week, and enrollment grew from a planned 920 to 2475, which should help power despite cluster randomization. The main risks are that many contacts are already infected at baseline, since swabs start on the dosing day, and that infections could be missed or diluted by the culture-based endpoint. These risks are partly offset by the strong pharmacology, giving a moderately high probability of success.

Standard rifaximin has strong evidence for secondary prevention of overt HE, but this new low-dose SSD formulation for primary prevention rests on a phase 2 whose primary endpoint failed and whose positive signal came from post hoc analyses. The population of ascites patients with no prior OHE has a low event rate, which limits power with about 517 patients over 72 weeks. I believe Bausch announced in early 2025 that this RED-C trial missed its primary endpoint, but even before readout the risk would have looked high. I would have forecast somewhere around 25–30%.

Orforglipron, an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist, produced large placebo-adjusted weight loss in Phase 2 (about 9-12% at 36 weeks), and later Phase 3 trials (ATTAIN-1, ACHIEVE-1) confirmed robust efficacy. With about 60 participants per arm, three active doses versus placebo, and a 72-week percent weight change endpoint, the trial is heavily overpowered for the expected effect of roughly 8-12% placebo-adjusted, even allowing for somewhat lower weight in Japanese patients. I don't specifically recall this Japan trial's readout, but failure would be very surprising given how consistent the GLP-1 class is on weight endpoints.

The first-listed primary outcome is baseline-adjusted measured (iohexol) GFR at 8 weeks, a mechanistic endpoint meant to show whether fenofibrate's known early eGFR drop reflects a true GFR reduction. If fenofibrate has any real acute effect, the plausible direction is a hemodynamic decline in GFR, which would not favor the drug; the other possibility is no difference, if the effect is only a creatinine artifact. A significant increase in iGFR, the only outcome that counts as success here, is mechanistically unlikely. With only 35 participants, a significant favorable result is improbable.

Troriluzole, a riluzole prodrug acting on glutamate, missed its primary endpoint in a Phase 2 adjunctive OCD trial and showed only a signal in post-hoc analyses of more severe patients. The primary endpoint here is restricted to the baseline Y-BOCS ≥24 cohort at week 8, which looks like enrichment built from that subgroup finding rather than a robustly validated effect. Adjunctive glutamatergic agents in OCD have generally failed, and psychiatric trials with high placebo response have low success rates. I have a vague sense that Biohaven's OCD program disappointed but no reliable recollection of this readout, so I put the probability somewhat below the Phase 3 psychiatry base rate.

Plasma kallikrein inhibition in DME has mixed prior evidence: KalVista's intravitreal KVD001 and Oxurion's THR-149 were largely disappointing versus anti-VEGF benchmarks. However, this trial compares an oral drug against placebo on an anatomic endpoint (CST) in a population with limited prior anti-VEGF exposure, and having three dose arms raises the odds that at least one comparison is significant. With about 23 patients per arm and noisy OCT measures, power is modest. I vaguely recall Rezolute reporting positive topline results in 2024, with significant placebo-adjusted CST reductions, which nudges this estimate up somewhat from a roughly 40-50% base rate.

The earlier phase 2 ladarixin trial in new-onset type 1 diabetes missed its C-peptide primary endpoint. This trial enriches for the low-residual-function subgroup that looked favourable only in a post hoc analysis, and such enrichment strategies seldom replicate. CXCR1/2 inhibition has little other clinical validation in type 1 diabetes, and immunomodulatory C-peptide trials have a low historical success rate. The larger-than-planned enrollment of 289 adds power, but the underlying effect is likely small or absent, so I place the probability well below the phase 2 base rate.

Pelacarsen consistently lowers Lp(a) by about 70–80% in phase 2 and HORIZON data. The primary endpoint, the rate of apheresis sessions, follows mechanically from Lp(a) levels, presumably because the protocol lets sessions be skipped once Lp(a) falls below a threshold, so even 51 patients should give ample power against placebo, whose patients would keep near-weekly sessions. The main risks are very high baseline Lp(a) in apheresis patients, which could keep many above the skip threshold, and German clinicians' reluctance to stop apheresis. I have no confident recall of the specific readout, but mechanism and design strongly favor success.

Bradykinin B2 receptor antagonism is a validated mechanism in HAE: icatibant works for acute attacks, and bradykinin is the final mediator of swelling. Continuous oral exposure to deucrictibant should give strong prophylaxis, and HAE prophylaxis trials such as berotralstat, lanadelumab and garadacimab typically show very large attack-rate reductions versus placebo. Even with about 10 patients per arm, a 70–85% reduction analyzed with a Poisson model would likely reach p<0.05, though the small sample and the US clinical hold add some risk. I recall the CHAPTER-1 topline (December 2023) reporting a significant reduction of roughly 80–85% in attack rate at the high dose, but I am setting the forecast from pre-readout reasoning.

Pemigatinib has strong single-arm second-line evidence in FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma (FIGHT-202), so a first-line PFS advantage over gemcitabine-cisplatin was biologically plausible. However, I recall that FIGHT-302, like other first-line FGFR-inhibitor trials (PROOF-301, FOENIX-CCA3), was discontinued early for slow enrollment in this rare molecular subset. Only 167 of roughly 430 planned patients were enrolled, and the transition-to-pemigatinib design suggests the randomized comparison was truncated and likely underpowered or only descriptive. A statistically significant PFS win is therefore unlikely.

This is ACHIEVE-5, a placebo-controlled add-on trial of orforglipron, an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist, on background insulin glargine, with HbA1c change at 40 weeks as the primary endpoint. GLP-1 agonists have reliably lowered HbA1c versus placebo in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, and orforglipron's phase 2 and ACHIEVE-1 data showed reductions of roughly 1.3–2%. With about 136 participants per arm and three doses, the trial is heavily powered for an effect of that size. I believe Lilly reported that ACHIEVE-5 met its primary endpoint, but a pre-readout forecast would already be near-certain.

BTK inhibition in CSU was already validated by Novartis's remibrutinib phase 2b, which showed large UAS7 reductions versus placebo. That makes it likely that an oral BTK inhibitor with three doses, about 40 patients per arm, and a continuous UAS7 change endpoint over 12 weeks would separate from placebo in at least one arm. The main risks are rilzabrutinib's reversible-covalent pharmacology and limited exposure at lower doses, plus the usual phase 2 placebo response. I recall Sanofi reporting that the highest dose (400 mg TID) met the UAS7 primary endpoint and that the program moved to phase 3, though I'd have put it around 0.75–0.8 beforehand.

Anti-tau antibodies aimed at extracellular or N-terminal and mid-region tau (gosuranemab, tilavonemab, zagotenemab, semorinemab in early AD) have repeatedly failed on clinical endpoints, so the base rate for this mechanism in a Phase 2 early-AD trial is very low. Posdinemab targets the p217+ mid-region epitope and enrolled a tau-PET-positive population, which is a plausible improvement. Still, about 520 participants split across three arms is underpowered to detect the modest iADRS effect such a drug would likely have. I recall that J&J announced in late 2025 that the AuTonomy trial missed its primary endpoint and discontinued the program, but my pre-readout estimate would have been roughly 8-10%.

Rocatinlimab (anti-OX40) showed significant EASI improvements over placebo in a well-sized phase 2b, and this phase 3 enrolls 769 patients with two dose arms against placebo monotherapy, which gives ample power even for modest effects on rIGA 0/1 and EASI-75 at week 24. The stricter rIGA endpoint and a placebo response of roughly 5–15% leave the treatment effect modest but still very likely significant at this sample size. I recall Amgen announcing in March 2024 that ROCKET-IGNITE met all co-primary and key secondary endpoints, though with a modest effect size; my pre-readout estimate would have been around 0.85–0.9.

Support for this trial comes from a small, mostly nonrandomized pilot suggesting sulindac reduces MRI breast density in women taking aromatase inhibitors, which is weak evidence for a placebo-controlled effect in a broader high-risk group. With about 61 participants and a modest expected effect on an imaging biomarker that varies from scan to scan, power is limited. Small academic phase II prevention trials on surrogate endpoints usually come out null. I don't recall this trial's result, so I sit somewhat below the typical phase II base rate.

Post-MI anti-remodeling trials using LVESVI as the endpoint have a poor track record, because modern PCI and guideline therapy already drive substantial spontaneous recovery, leaving little room for a drug effect. CDR132L, a miR-132 antisense oligonucleotide, had only small phase 1b data in chronic HF and preclinical support, so efficacy evidence in humans was thin. With about 98 patients per arm and noisy echo volumes, the trial was powered only for a moderate effect. I recall that HF-REVERT was reported, after Novo Nordisk acquired Cardior, as not meeting its primary LVESVI endpoint, and this lines up with the low prior.

The Phase 1/2 study of DTX401 showed large, durable reductions in cornstarch requirements, and the mechanism (AAV8 liver-directed G6Pase replacement) directly targets the primary endpoint, percent change in daily cornstarch intake. Against a placebo arm with no expected change, 52 patients gives ample power for an effect of that size, although the endpoint depends on clinician-guided titration, which adds some variability. I recall Ultragenyx announcing positive topline results in 2024, with roughly a 41% cornstarch reduction versus about 10% on placebo (highly significant). Setting that aside, the pre-readout estimate would still have been high.

LY4100511 (DC-853) is DICE's second-generation oral small-molecule IL-17A inhibitor. Its predecessor DC-806 already showed a significant PASI-75 benefit over placebo (about 44% vs 13%) in phase 1b, so the mechanism has clinical validation, and DC-853 was reportedly chosen for better exposure. PASI-75 versus placebo at week 12, with roughly 55 patients per arm and three doses, is a forgiving endpoint: placebo response is usually under 10–15%, and any moderately active agent clears significance. The main risks are inadequate potency or PK of the oral molecule, or a program deprioritization, so I sit somewhat below the rate for validated psoriasis mechanisms.

Complement inhibition has a plausible mechanism in HSCT-TMA, and eculizumab and ravulizumab showed encouraging single-arm results, mostly in children. But adult HSCT-TMA is heterogeneous, and deaths from GVHD, infection and relapse are common and largely independent of complement, which dilutes the composite event-free survival endpoint; best supportive care in the placebo arm also lets some patients improve. A trial of about 148 patients with a noisy laboratory-based worsening composite carries substantial risk, so I would have put success somewhat below even. I believe AstraZeneca/Alexion later reported that the adult trial did not meet its primary endpoint, but this forecast reflects the pre-readout view.

This is a small investigator-initiated phase II trial (TBCRC 056) in which roughly 20 TNBC patients per arm were randomized to niraparib plus dostarlimab versus a 3-week niraparib lead-in. The first primary endpoint is the change in TILs at 3 weeks, and any between-arm comparison of a noisy biomarker at this sample size is underpowered. The record does not make clear whether the prespecified test is between arms or a within-arm change from baseline, and a within-arm increase is more plausible to reach significance. Weighing that ambiguity against the low power, I estimate about a 30% chance of a clearly positive primary result.

Anti-CD20 therapy already has strong randomized evidence in steroid-dependent and frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome. In Basu et al. (2018), rituximab clearly beat MMF on 12-month relapse-free survival, and obinutuzumab gives deeper B-cell depletion. The main risks are the small sample (n=85), an active comparator, and a strict composite endpoint requiring steroid withdrawal, but the expected effect size makes success likely. I believe Roche announced in 2025 that INShore met its primary endpoint, though my forecast relies mainly on the prior evidence.

This is a small, single-site, unblinded pilot phase II (planned n=80) comparing tailored versus usual-care prednisone dosing within R-CHOP, with a log-rank comparison of hyperglycemia incidence after 3 cycles. Cutting the glucocorticoid dose should plausibly lower glucose, but 'tailored' reduction likely kicks in only after hyperglycemia appears, which would blunt any difference in cumulative incidence. Pilot trials like this are usually underpowered and often under-enroll. A statistically significant primary result therefore looks unlikely.

Anti-IL-13 therapy had already shown weak efficacy in asthma, where lebrikizumab's Phase 3 LAVOLTA program was inconsistent, and there was no prior evidence of FEV1 benefit in COPD. At the time, type-2 inflammation in COPD was a speculative target. With roughly 300 patients split by biomarker status, the trial has limited power to detect the small FEV1 change that IL-13 blockade would plausibly produce at Week 12. I vaguely recall that this trial showed no significant FEV1 improvement and that Roche dropped respiratory development of lebrikizumab, so I put the probability low.

Repurposing trials in PAD that target muscle metabolism with a six-minute walk primary endpoint have usually been null; McDermott's group has run many such academic trials and most did not meet their endpoints. The rationale for metformin (mitochondrial and AMPK effects in nondiabetic patients) is mainly preclinical, and with about 200 participants the trial can detect only a moderate effect. I recall that PERMET reported no significant improvement in six-minute walk distance with metformin versus placebo, but my forecast rests on the low base rate and weak prior evidence.

Older randomized trials from the 1980s–90s showed IVIG reduced bacterial infections in hypogammaglobulinemic CLL, which gives the mechanism some support. However, under modern targeted CLL therapies, COVID-era conduct and broad anti-infective prophylaxis, major-infection event rates are likely low, and 247 patients over about one year may lack power on a binary endpoint. My vague recollection is that PRO-SID did not show a statistically significant reduction in major infections, but even setting that aside, a low-event, underpowered placebo-controlled design warrants a below-base-rate estimate.

Apraclonidine is a potent alpha-2 agonist, and alpha agonists such as brimonidine 0.025% (Lumify) reliably produce large vasoconstrictive reductions in ocular redness compared with vehicle, typically with p<0.0001. Alcon is running this Phase 3 as a registration study with an Ora-style hyperemia model, and about 80 subjects per arm is more than enough for the expected effect size. The main risk is the co-primary 10-hour endpoint, since durability at 10 hours with a 0.125% concentration is less certain, though apraclonidine's duration and Lumify's 8-hour data make success likely.

Switch studies in virologically suppressed people with HIV using the FDA snapshot outcome of HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL with a non-inferiority margin (typically 4%) almost always succeed, because failure rates in both arms are very low. Bictegravir is a high-barrier integrase inhibitor, lenacapavir is a potent capsid inhibitor, and people with bictegravir resistance were excluded. The Phase 2 portion already showed comparable suppression, and I recall Gilead announcing in 2025 that the Phase 3 ARTISTRY-1 met its non-inferiority primary endpoint at week 48. Even without that recollection, the base rate for this design would put success above 90%.

TAK-101 (formerly TIMP-GLIA/CNP-101) reduced gliadin-specific IFN-γ ELISpot responses after gluten challenge in an earlier Phase 2a study, which gives this mechanistic biomarker endpoint some prior support. Against that, the earlier signal came from a small trial, and ELISpot readouts are noisy, especially with small per-arm samples (about 18 per active arm versus a pooled placebo group). I have a vague recollection that Takeda later dropped TAK-101 from its pipeline, which would suggest disappointing Phase 2 results, but I don't reliably recall the primary-endpoint outcome. Balancing the supportive prior data against the small size and the possible discontinuation, I put the chance of success below even.

This looks like LAVOLTA I, one of two replicate Phase III lebrikizumab trials. As I recall, LAVOLTA I showed a significant exacerbation reduction in the prespecified biomarker-high (periostin/eosinophil) primary population and LAVOLTA II did not. Before readout, Phase II (LUTE/VERSE) evidence for a periostin-high effect, two doses and a large sample made success plausible, but the overall effect was modest and inconsistent, so a careful analyst would have put this near a coin flip. There is also uncertainty about whether the registry's primary analysis is the biomarker-high or the overall population, which tempers a forecast that would otherwise be higher.

K-645 is an oral acute migraine agent from a small, newly formed company, and its mechanism is not public, so it gets little benefit from validated-target precedent. Pain freedom at 2 hours is a hard endpoint: placebo rates run around 15-20% and even proven gepants and triptans add only about 5-15 points. The within-subject 3-period crossover with about 134 patients and two doses improves power, and either dose succeeding counts. Weighing a modest base rate for novel-mechanism phase 2a acute migraine trials against the efficient design, I estimate somewhat below even odds.

Before readout, the evidence was mixed. Astegolimab, an anti-ST2 (IL-33 pathway) antibody, missed its primary endpoint in the Phase 2a COPD-ST2OP trial but showed exacerbation signals, and other IL-33 pathway agents such as itepekimab had shown mixed results in COPD. ALIENTO is large (about 1,300 patients across two dose arms) and enrolls frequent exacerbators, which gives it reasonable power to detect a modest 15–20% reduction in exacerbation rate, but COPD exacerbation trials frequently fall just short of significance. I recall that ALIENTO reportedly reached significance on the Q2W arm (about a 15% reduction) while the companion Phase 3 ARNASA missed; my pre-readout estimate is near 45%.

AD109 (aroxybutynin/atomoxetine) targets upper-airway muscle tone through a well-supported mechanism, and the Phase 2b MARIPOSA trial showed statistically significant AHI reductions versus placebo, though some secondary endpoints were mixed. With 646 patients, a placebo control, an objective PSG-based AHI endpoint and a moderate-severity population, this trial is well powered to detect the effect sizes seen in Phase 2. The main risks are attenuation of the effect over 6 months and placebo or regression-to-the-mean noise in AHI. I recall that Apnimed announced in 2025 that SynAIRgy met its primary endpoint, but my pre-readout estimate would have been about 0.77.

In PBC, OCA and bezafibrate each lower ALP substantially through complementary mechanisms (FXR agonism and PPAR agonism), and earlier data suggested at least additive ALP effects, so the combination arms should plausibly beat bezafibrate monotherapy on change in ALP. Against that, bezafibrate alone is an active control with a large effect, and the arms are small (about 19 participants each), which limits power to detect the incremental benefit over only 12 weeks. ALP is a sensitive, low-variance biochemical endpoint that moves quickly, and either combination arm succeeding counts, which raises the odds. I do not clearly recall the topline result of this specific trial, so I estimate a moderately favourable probability.

The primary endpoint is a safety comparison: the number of participants with grade 3 or higher adverse events through week 24, in a small open-label trial of about 56 per arm. Adding metformin to standard TB treatment is very unlikely to produce significantly fewer severe adverse events than standard treatment alone, so a superiority 'win' in the favorable direction is improbable. The most likely outcome is similar rates, with the investigators calling metformin safe and well tolerated. Some residual probability allows for the result being scored as met on safety grounds, or for chance imbalances.

Phase 2 trials in MCI and early Alzheimer's disease have a very low success rate, and nicotinic agonists have repeatedly failed to show durable cognitive benefit over long treatment periods. The pilot evidence for transdermal nicotine in MCI came from a small, 6-month study (Newhouse 2012), and the trial enrolled fewer participants than planned (348 vs 380). It also relies on a single Cogstate list-learning endpoint over 24 months. I believe the MIND results, presented around 2023–2024, showed no benefit of nicotine over placebo on the primary outcome, but even before readout a low probability was warranted.

LY3541860 is understood to be a B-cell-depleting (anti-CD19) antibody, and B-cell depletion has a strong track record of rapidly and dramatically suppressing new gadolinium-enhancing lesions in relapsing MS (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, ublituximab phase 2 data). A 12-week cumulative new GdE lesion count against placebo is a sensitive endpoint that phase 2 MS trials of effective mechanisms usually meet. The main concerns are the small enrollment (65, possibly truncated from an adaptive 2a/2b plan), the short 12-week window during which onset may not be complete, and uncertainty about whether the program continued. On balance the mechanism supports a better-than-base-rate chance of success.

IncobotulinumtoxinA (Xeomin) already had positive phase 3 data for platysma prominence on the MAPS scale, and botulinum toxins produce large, reliable effects on dynamic muscle-band severity scores against placebo. The primary endpoint is a continuous change from baseline at week 2, near peak effect, judged by the investigator, which gives good power even with about 18 subjects per arm. Only one of three doses needs to beat placebo. The main risks are the small sample and an unusually strong placebo response, so the forecast stays a little below certainty.

Rifaximin itself works for secondary OHE prevention, but the low-dose SSD formulation for primary prevention rests on a weak Phase 2 signal. That study missed its primary endpoint and showed only post hoc benefit at 40mg IR. Primary prevention in patients with controlled ascites and no prior OHE yields few events, and a composite including death dilutes the drug effect, so power is a concern even with 524 patients. I believe Bausch announced in 2025 that the first RED-C Phase 3 trial missed its primary endpoint, so I am forecasting low, consistent with the pre-readout skepticism.

This is the CLARION-CKD trial of KBP-5074 (ocedurenone). Phase 2 BLOCK-CKD data suggested meaningful SBP lowering, which would normally support a moderate-to-favorable prior for a placebo-controlled BP endpoint. However, the record itself states the trial was terminated after an IDMC futility determination. I also recall that Novo Nordisk stopped the ocedurenone program in 2024 because the trial was unlikely to meet its primary endpoint, so the probability of a significant result on Week 12 SBP is very low.

Colchicine's evidence for preventing postoperative AF comes mainly from cardiac surgery and is mixed (COPPS positive, COPPS-2 neutral), and thoracic surgery has lower event rates (~7-10% clinically important AF) and possibly different mechanisms. A 3,200-patient trial is powered only for a fairly large relative reduction, which is optimistic for an anti-inflammatory approach, and the strict 'clinically important AF' definition lowers event counts further. I recall the Lancet 2023 publication: neither co-primary outcome was significant (AF about 6.4% vs 7.5%, MINS about 18% vs 21%), so the trial missed. My pre-readout estimate, ignoring that recall, would have been roughly 25-30%.

Prevention trials for cardiac-surgery-associated AKI have almost all failed, and complement C5 inhibition has no prior randomized evidence of reducing MAKE90 in CKD patients undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass. The composite endpoint is diluted by components (≥25% eGFR decline, death, KRT) that complement blockade may not affect much, and 555 patients gives limited power for a modest effect. I believe AstraZeneca/Alexion reported that ARTEMIS did not meet its primary endpoint, but on the pre-readout evidence alone I would have put success at roughly 15–20%.

Perioperative PD-(L)1 blockade added to platinum chemotherapy has a strong class record in resectable NSCLC: CheckMate 816, KEYNOTE-671, AEGEAN, Neotorch and RATIONALE-315 all met their EFS endpoints, and atezolizumab already succeeded in the adjuvant setting (IMpower010). That supports a prior well above the oncology phase 3 base rate, tempered by the modest enrollment of 453 and possible dilution from enrolling stage II patients and mixed chemotherapy backbones. I recall that Roche reported IMpower030 did not meet its EFS primary endpoint. The pre-readout estimate is still about 0.7.

I have a vague recollection that RTB-004 showed no significant difference between tocilizumab and placebo on the 1-year composite endpoint; the probability below is a pre-readout estimate. Before the readout, the base rate for phase 2 add-on immunomodulators in solid-organ transplant is low, because standard triple immunosuppression already keeps rejection rates fairly low. The composite is driven largely by dnDSA and mild rejection, which makes it noisy. With about 200 randomized patients, only a large effect would reach significance, and IL-6 blockade had limited prior evidence in heart transplant beyond small kidney desensitization and chronic AMR data.

Lebrikizumab's evidence in asthma was mixed: MILLY showed modest FEV1 gains in ICS-treated patients, but the phase 2 study in steroid-naive patients (Noonan 2013) found no significant FEV1 benefit over placebo. Anti-IL-13 monotherapy on pre-bronchodilator FEV1 over 12 weeks, with about 100 patients per arm and no biomarker enrichment, needs an effect of roughly 100+ mL that earlier data do not support. Adding a montelukast assay-sensitivity arm suggests the sponsor expected small effects. I recall this trial (Korenblat et al.) did not show a significant FEV1 improvement for lebrikizumab versus placebo; my pre-readout estimate would still have been low, around 25%.

Trials aiming to regress fibrosis in compensated NASH cirrhosis have a poor track record (simtuzumab, selonsertib STELLAR-4, belapectin, emricasan), and with only about 60 patients per arm, 36 weeks may be too short to show regression in F4. Efruxifermin had strong F2–F3 histology data from HARMONY and a small encouraging cirrhotic cohort in BALANCED, which raises the odds above the base rate. Even so, the arms are underpowered for the modest placebo-adjusted effect plausible at week 36. I recall the week-36 primary endpoint was not statistically significant (about 22% vs 14%), with significance emerging only at week 96.

This is SKYSCRAPER-01. Before readout, the case for it rested on the randomized phase II CITYSCAPE trial, where tiragolumab plus atezolizumab showed large ORR and PFS gains in PD-L1-high patients. However, CITYSCAPE was small (n=135), and TIGIT had no prior phase III validation, so a CITYSCAPE-sized effect was unlikely to replicate in full. Add-on-to-IO phase III trials in NSCLC have a poor track record (e.g., epacadostat, CTLA-4 combos), so a moderate probability of roughly 35% is reasonable; I recall that the trial in fact missed its PFS co-primary endpoint.

In the Phase 2b B-Clear trial, bepirovirsen produced sustained HBsAg loss with HBV DNA suppression in about 9-10% of NA-treated patients, with higher rates at low baseline HBsAg. Spontaneous functional cure on placebo plus NA after stopping NA is near 0-1%. Enriching for baseline HBsAg ≤3000 IU/mL and enrolling about 430 per arm gives very high power, even if the effect shrinks in Phase 3. The main risks were attrition and the stringent off-treatment cure definition. I recall GSK announcing that B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 met their primary endpoints, but this estimate reflects the pre-readout evidence.

This is a small (n=39), single-center, investigator-initiated phase 2 trial testing whether 6 months of sacubitril/valsartan changes ECV by cardiac MRI in people with HIV who have subclinical myocardial dysfunction. ECV changes slowly and the trial is underpowered for modest effects, so a significant between-group difference is unlikely; PARAMOUNT-like HFpEF data showed LA volume benefits, but over longer periods and in larger samples. Enrollment probably fell short of target given the COVID-era start, which further reduces power. I don't recall the specific result, and the base rate for small mechanistic imaging-endpoint trials suggests roughly a 20% chance of success on the first primary endpoint.

Prevention trials in critical care, especially those testing repurposed inhaled therapies for ARDS or acute respiratory failure, have a very low historical success rate, and the LIPS-B pilot of inhaled budesonide/formoterol showed only modest oxygenation effects, not hard-outcome benefit. The composite ARF endpoint depends on clinician-driven escalation, and background dexamethasone use in COVID-19 patients likely dilutes any steroid effect. Enrollment of 465 appears to fall short of the original target, which suggests early stopping or reduced power. I vaguely recall the trial did not show a significant reduction in acute respiratory failure, but my forecast rests mainly on the low prior.

This is a small (n=33), single-site, open-label phase 2 trial comparing two active buprenorphine formulations, and the effect on days of opioid use per week is likely modest. The pivotal trial (Lofwall 2018, CAM2038) showed only non-inferiority with a modest superiority signal, while in practice Sublocade's advantages are mostly adherence and retention. In fentanyl users, induction difficulty and dropout will add noise, and the study was disrupted by the NIH/OHRP research suspension, which further undermines power. Statistical significance on the primary endpoint is therefore unlikely, though possible given Sublocade's higher steady-state buprenorphine levels.

This is a three-arm, roughly 65-per-arm window-of-opportunity trial in ER+ invasive lobular carcinoma testing whether fulvestrant suppresses Ki67 more than anastrozole or tamoxifen. Prior data (IMPACT, the fulvestrant 500 mg studies) suggest AIs and fulvestrant both suppress Ki67 more than tamoxifen, so a fulvestrant-versus-tamoxifen difference is plausible, but a fulvestrant-versus-anastrozole difference is unlikely to reach significance. Within-arm Ki67 reductions from baseline will almost certainly be significant, but the prespecified between-arm hypothesis is the harder bar. Weighing the ambiguity over which comparison counts against the likely failure versus anastrozole, I land near even odds.

Cocaine use disorder pharmacotherapy trials have an extremely poor track record: almost every Phase 2 trial has failed, and no drug is approved. Here an 82-subject trial uses a demanding binary endpoint, continuous abstinence over weeks 11–13 confirmed by urine benzoylecgonine, which typically leaves very low event rates and little power. Support for the metyrapone/oxazepam mechanism is limited to small human laboratory studies, and I don't recall a positive topline announcement from Embera, which suggests failure.

Demonstrating superiority over quetiapine XR, an approved and effective adjunctive treatment that also strongly helps insomnia, is a high bar. Seltorexant's placebo-controlled adjunctive MDD data show only modest effects, roughly 2 MADRS points, so beating an active comparator on a binary 26-week response endpoint is unlikely. The likely winning case for the sponsor is tolerability: better retention and less weight gain, which could favor seltorexant on a discontinuation-affected responder analysis. My recollection is that seltorexant was numerically similar or slightly better but did not reach statistical superiority on the primary endpoint, while showing clear tolerability advantages.

This is the ARGO trial. MoonLake reported in late 2023 that sonelokimab met the ACR50 primary endpoint at week 12, with roughly 46% versus 20% for placebo. Before readout, the IL-17A/F mechanism already had strong validation in PsA (bimekizumab's phase 3 wins), and sonelokimab had shown strong psoriasis data. With about 40 patients per arm, ACR50 versus placebo at week 12 in a mostly biologic-naive population gives high power, and three doses offer multiple chances to succeed, so I would have forecast about 0.9 even without knowing the result.

This is a small, single-site academic mechanistic Phase 2 trial testing whether tadalafil induces beiging of subcutaneous white fat in obese adults, with MRI fat signal fraction as the first primary endpoint. Rodent data support PDE5 inhibition promoting browning, but human translation of browning interventions has generally been weak. Thermoneutral FSF in subcutaneous WAT of obese people is a hard endpoint to shift meaningfully in 12 weeks. With about 50 per arm and a modest plausible effect, a null result seems more likely than a significant one.

This is a small (n=29) single-site, investigator-initiated open-label study of metformin against observation, with an immunologic surrogate endpoint (PD-1+TIGIT+ CD4 T cells) measured over 72 weeks. The Lilac pilot (ACTG A5326) hinted that metformin might reduce PD-1/TIGIT co-expression, but effects were modest, and pilot signals often fail to replicate in randomized comparisons this underpowered. With perhaps 12–14 evaluable participants per arm and noisy flow-cytometry measures, a statistically significant between-arm difference is unlikely, though possible if the effect is real.

Apraclonidine is an established alpha-adrenergic agonist with strong vasoconstrictive effects, and the analogous low-dose brimonidine (Lumify) beat vehicle by wide margins on the same Ora Calibra redness scale. The 15-minute and 1-hour co-primaries should be easy wins against vehicle. The 10-hour adult co-primary is the main risk, but Alcon likely picked it from earlier-phase durability data, which supports a long-duration claim. With about 284 subjects and a large expected effect, the odds of all co-primaries succeeding are high, tempered mainly by the 10-hour endpoint.

Prophylactic HPV vaccines do not clear existing infections. The closest analog, the AMC-072 trial of quadrivalent vaccine against anal HSIL in HIV-positive adults, found no benefit, and randomized trials of vaccination after LEEP (VACCIN, NOVEL) have been largely null. Here the primary endpoint is HSIL recurrence at weeks 4–52, a window where recurrence comes mostly from persistent existing infections that a prophylactic vaccine cannot affect, and the trial has only about 535 participants. I vaguely recall COVENANT reporting no significant reduction, which fits this prior, so the probability is low.

CT-868 is a daily GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, and incretin agonists in type 1 diabetes have produced only modest HbA1c reductions versus placebo (about 0.2–0.4% with liraglutide in the ADJUNCT trials), partly because investigators lower insulin doses to avoid hypoglycemia. This trial has roughly 28 participants per arm over 16 weeks, so it is only moderately powered unless the true effect is around 0.4–0.5%. That effect is plausible in overweight patients with baseline HbA1c of 7–10%, and earlier Phase 1b T1D data and Roche's acquisition of the drug suggest some biological signal. Three dose arms give multiple chances for a significant result, but the small sample and insulin-titration dilution keep this close to a coin flip.

High-concentration capsaicin has shown modest, inconsistent separation from the 0.04% low-dose control: postherpetic neuralgia trials were positive, but several HIV-neuropathy trials failed. Neuropathic pain Phase III trials have high placebo responses and frequent failures, and the burning from the active low-dose control helps keep the blind, which makes separation harder. There are two regulator-specific primary analyses (an average over weeks 2–12 and the week-12 value), and the US MMRM analysis at a single timepoint is more demanding. I vaguely recall that Grünenthal/Averitas reported this PSNP trial missed its primary endpoint, so I lean below a neutral base rate.

Small (n=40), open-label, single-site Phase II trials of novel add-on agents in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer usually fail, so the base rate is low. This record, however, was registered retrospectively in 2023, nearly four years after the 2019 start, by a small sponsor. That pattern suggests the data were already in hand and looked favorable. I have a vague memory of a CureLab publication reporting significantly longer PFS with Elenagen plus gemcitabine than with gemcitabine alone, which pushes the estimate up despite the small sample and the risk of unblinded assessment bias.

This is OASIS 2: oral semaglutide 50 mg versus placebo in East Asian adults with overweight or obesity. The STEP 6 trial of injectable semaglutide in East Asians and OASIS 1 of oral 50 mg both showed large weight-loss differences over placebo, roughly 10 percentage points or more. With about 200 participants randomised 3:1, a 68-week treatment period and a placebo comparator, power for both co-primary endpoints is overwhelming. I believe the reported result was about -11% versus -2%, consistent with success, but the forecast rests mainly on the strong prior evidence.

Edonerpic maleate (T-817MA) already failed its earlier phase 2 trial (US202) in mild-to-moderate AD on cognitive endpoints, and this trial appears to rest on an exploratory signal of CSF p-tau181 reduction from that study. Non-amyloid, putatively neuroprotective small molecules have a very poor record of moving CSF p-tau, and exploratory biomarker signals often fail to replicate. A CSF p-tau endpoint with about 220 patients over 78 weeks is reasonably powered if the effect is real, which keeps the probability from being very low. Weak mechanistic support and the prior failure still argue for a low estimate.

Retatrutide's glucagon-receptor agonism plus large weight loss is expected to raise GFR acutely, and post-hoc analyses of the retatrutide phase 2 obesity data reportedly showed eGFR increases. Indexing to BSA should also inflate indexed mGFR as body size shrinks over 24 weeks. Counterpoints: semaglutide's REMODEL did not clearly change mGFR, iohexol mGFR is noisy, and n≈146 gives only moderate power. The direction of the hypothesis is also somewhat ambiguous, but a significant increase would likely be framed as the positive outcome.

This is a small (23 enrolled versus 60 planned), single-center, open-label pilot of IV digoxin in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, and its secondary outcomes are mostly about feasibility. The primary endpoint is day-3 change in highly variable cytokines (IL-6, IL-10, TNF-alpha), and with roughly 11 patients per arm the trial has very little power to show a significant difference. The only support for the mechanism comes from preclinical work, and earlier anti-inflammatory approaches in alcoholic hepatitis, such as anti-TNF therapy, have had disappointing clinical results. A significant favorable result is unlikely, though multiple cytokines and a lack of multiplicity correction leave a small chance one comes out positive.

This is a small, single-site, pilot-style phase 2 study (its primary aim is described as collecting preliminary data), looking at whether high-dose vitamin D with or without exercise changes BMD over 24 weeks in women on aromatase inhibitors. Six months is short for detecting BMD differences by DXA. The control arm also gets calcium and a multivitamin, and vitamin D supplementation trials in mildly deficient populations have mostly shown little or no BMD benefit.
