Home-based walking and resistance-band programs likewise rarely produce significant BMD changes in this timeframe, so the chance of a significant result in favour of an investigational arm is low.

This trial is AERIFY-1. My recollection is that Sanofi announced in 2025 that it met its primary endpoint, with roughly a 27% exacerbation reduction in former smokers, while the sister trial AERIFY-2 failed. Before the readout, the main support was a phase 2 trial that missed its primary endpoint but showed about a 42% exacerbation reduction in a post hoc former-smoker subgroup. Subgroup-derived hypotheses often fail to replicate, and other anti-IL-33/ST2 programs in COPD had mixed results, but the large sample, two dose arms and a validated endpoint give a fair chance, so I would have put it near a coin flip.

Sonelokimab is a nanobody that blocks both IL-17A and IL-17F, the same targets as bimekizumab, which produced large HiSCR effects in HS in phase 2 and phase 3. That gives strong mechanistic support for beating placebo on HiSCR75. Each arm has about 58 patients, and placebo HiSCR75 rates are typically around 10-20%, so the trial is well powered for the effect sizes seen with IL-17 agents; the stringent HiSCR75 endpoint and the multi-dose design add only modest risk. I recall that the MIRA trial reported a significant HiSCR75 benefit for the 120 mg dose, but my forecast reflects the strong prior from the evidence available before readout.

Sjögren's phase 2 trials have a poor historical record because of high placebo responses on ESSDAI-type endpoints, though several recent biologics (ianalumab, dazodalibep, iscalimab) have shown signals. FcRn blockade lowering pathogenic IgG autoantibodies is mechanistically plausible in an anti-Ro-positive population, but there was no prior efficacy evidence in this disease, and about 54 patients per arm is modest for a continuous clinESSDAI endpoint. Two dose arms and Janssen's execution help somewhat, so a pre-readout estimate near 40% is reasonable. I recall the DAHLIAS topline reporting that the 15 mg/kg dose met the clinESSDAI primary endpoint, but this probability reflects only what was knowable before the readout.

This is a small single-site VA trial (n=114) with three arms, and the right comparison to score is ambiguous. Against the healthy-lifestyle-plus-metformin arm, the lifestyle-plus-metformin arm would almost certainly improve PPT significantly, since Villareal's prior lifestyle trials showed gains of about 2–3 points. Against lifestyle plus placebo, which is the key placebo-controlled comparison, metformin's added benefit is speculative and may even blunt exercise gains, as MASTERS suggested, so success there is maybe 20–30%. Weighting the uncertainty over which comparison counts as primary gives roughly a coin flip.

This is an open-label, single-group-style pilot with no control arm. It tests dietary supplements (astaxanthin, Protandim, melatonin, MitoQ) in ALS, a disease where antioxidant and supplement approaches have repeatedly failed. With 50 participants split across four categories and a lead-in self-control comparing ALSFRS-R slope pre- versus post-treatment, a statistically significant slowing is unlikely, and the pilot is probably descriptive without a formal hypothesis test. Even under a lenient reading, the base rate for showing efficacy here is very low.

Phase 3 IPF trials have a poor historical success rate, and inhaled treprostinil's antifibrotic evidence before the readout rested mainly on a post-hoc FVC signal from the INCREASE trial in ILD-associated pulmonary hypertension, plus preclinical antifibrotic data for prostacyclins. On the other hand, absolute FVC change over 52 weeks with about 600 patients is well powered for a moderate effect, and background antifibrotics are allowed, so the comparison is against standard of care plus placebo. I recall that TETON-2 and TETON-1 were both reported as positive on FVC, but the pre-readout estimate should stay near even odds given the mechanistic uncertainty and the field's track record.

Orforglipron, an oral non-peptide GLP-1 agonist, produced up to about 14.7% mean weight loss versus 2.3% for placebo at 36 weeks in its Phase 2 obesity trial, and GLP-1 agonists reliably beat placebo on percent weight change. With about 3,100 participants, three doses and a 72-week placebo-controlled design, statistical power on the primary endpoint is essentially certain. I recall that ATTAIN-1 reported about 12.4% mean weight loss at 36 mg versus about 0.9% on placebo, with all doses significant, though my pre-readout estimate would have been nearly as high anyway. The only real risk was operational failure such as extreme dropout, which is very unlikely.

Suvorexant has established efficacy for total sleep time in primary insomnia, and the same Hopkins group's earlier inpatient opioid-withdrawal pilot reported improved sleep, which supports the mechanism. However, this is an outpatient trial pooled across three different MAT groups, and the primary outcome is actigraphy/diary total sleep time. Actigraphy is less sensitive than polysomnography, and diary measures carry large placebo responses, so the expected effect of about 15–25 minutes may be hard to detect with roughly 80 completers per arm. Investigator-initiated phase 2 trials in addiction populations often miss, so I lean slightly below even odds.

Pegvaliase is an approved enzyme substitution therapy. In the adult PRISM trials it produced large, durable blood Phe reductions, with many patients reaching near-normal levels by one year, and the mechanism should work the same way in adolescents. The comparator is diet-only in patients already failing to control Phe above 600 μmol/L, so the control arm should change little, and with 72 weeks for titration even 36 vs 18 participants gives ample power for the expected effect. Risks are dropouts from hypersensitivity reactions and slower responders, but I recall BioMarin reporting that this adolescent study met its primary endpoint, which fits a high prior.

This is a small (n=43) single-site NIAAA-funded pilot of pregabalin versus placebo in AUD, with heavy drinking days by TLFB as the primary outcome. Prior evidence is mixed: some European trials suggest benefit, and gabapentin's results are inconsistent. Small placebo-controlled AUD trials usually fail to reach significance because placebo response is large and power is low. Disruptions from the research pause and early stopping, with enrollment below the planned 50, lower the chances further, though a longitudinal weekly-HDD mixed model gives some added power.

Phentolamine 0.75% (Nyxol) reliably constricts the pupil. In the earlier LYNX-1 Phase 3 trial, the ≥15-letter mesopic low-contrast acuity responder endpoint favored drug numerically but missed significance. LYNX-2 enriches for likely responders (pupil ≥5 mm, ≥10-letter gain with the brightness acuity tester) and moves the primary timepoint to Day 15, both of which should raise the drug–placebo gap. With about 200 patients and an expected responder difference of roughly 10 percentage points against a low placebo rate, power is moderate, so I put success somewhat above even. I believe the sponsor later announced that LYNX-2 met its primary endpoint, but the forecast reflects pre-readout uncertainty.

Gaboxadol is a potent extrasynaptic GABA-A agonist with well-documented EEG effects, such as increased slow-wave and theta activity, so a pharmacodynamic target-engagement signal at 60 minutes is mechanistically plausible. However, the trial has only 10 participants and is split across home and lab sessions. The primary outcome spans several frequency bands without a clearly prespecified single test. Resting-state EEG in FXS is noisy, and single-dose effects at 10 mg may be modest, so a statistically significant result on the first-listed measure is close to a coin flip.

This is Moderna's P304 efficacy trial of mRNA-1010 against standard-dose Fluarix in adults 50 and older. Before the readout, the supporting evidence was the P303 immunogenicity data, where mRNA-1010 showed superior HAI titers for the A strains and noninferior titers for B, and the 40,000-participant case-driven design gave good power for a modest relative vaccine efficacy. The main risks were that HAI gains might not translate into clinical protection, that B-strain performance was weaker, and that season and strain-match variability could hurt; earlier mRNA-1010 efficacy attempts had also been mixed. I recall Moderna announcing in mid-2025 that the trial showed superior relative vaccine efficacy (about 27%), but the probability I would have given beforehand is moderately favorable, around 0.66.

MC4R agonism is strongly validated in acquired hypothalamic obesity: setmelanotide produced large BMI reductions in phase 2 and in the phase 3 TRANSCEND trial, so an oral MC4R agonist from the same sponsor has a plausible path to a big effect. The main risk is the small sample (about 7 per arm), but a large effect in HO, where placebo patients typically gain weight, should still give significance for at least one dose at 14 weeks. Uncertainty remains about the oral drug's potency and exposure compared with setmelanotide. I recall Rhythm reporting a statistically significant, dose-dependent BMI reduction in mid-2025, but my pre-readout estimate is about 0.8.

This Phase 2 trial compares non-fluoride arginine dentifrices with an 1100 ppm fluoride active control, and the record does not say whether the primary DMFS-increment comparison is non-inferiority or superiority. Beating fluoride with arginine alone over only 12 months is unlikely, because one-year DMFS increments are small and noisy even with about 500 children per arm. Earlier Colgate data (Acevedo et al.) suggested non-fluoride arginine may roughly match fluoride, so a non-inferiority success is plausible if that margin is the prespecified test. Weighing the uncertainty about design against the low chance of a superiority win, I put the probability of a topline-style success at about 35%.

Epcoritamab has strong single-arm activity in R/R DLBCL, and glofitamab-GemOx (STARGLO) beat R-GemOx on overall survival, so there is mechanistic support. However, this trial tests epcoritamab monotherapy, and overall survival is a hard endpoint in an open-label trial. Crossover to commercial bispecifics or CAR-T after progression on the chemo arm, especially at US sites, could dilute any survival difference. Weighing these, I would have put the pre-readout probability somewhat below even. I recall Genmab announcing that the trial did not reach statistical significance on overall survival.

Baxdrostat, an aldosterone synthase inhibitor, already showed placebo-adjusted systolic reductions of roughly 9–11 mmHg in BrigHTN and BaxHTN, and ambulatory BP removes much of the placebo and white-coat noise. With about 109 patients per arm, a 24-hour ABPM effect of even 6–8 mmHg would be detected with high power. The mechanism is well validated in resistant hypertension (cf. spironolactone in PATHWAY-2), so the main risk is execution rather than efficacy. I recall AstraZeneca reported that Bax24 met its primary endpoint with a large placebo-adjusted reduction in 24-hour systolic BP, but even without that the pre-readout forecast would be very high.

Itepekimab's phase 2 COPD trial missed its overall primary endpoint, but a post hoc subgroup of former smokers showed about a 42% reduction in exacerbations. That made this phase 3 trial, restricted to former smokers, an enrichment bet built on a subgroup finding, which historically replicates only modestly. In its favour, dupilumab's success in COPD validates type 2 and alarmin biology, the sample is large (about 1,100 patients over 52 weeks), and two dose arms give two chances to succeed. I recall that AERIFY-1 met its primary endpoint (about 27% reduction) while its sister trial AERIFY-2 failed, but my pre-readout estimate would have been roughly a coin flip.

AXS-05 (dextromethorphan-bupropion) had a positive Phase 2/3 ADVANCE-1 on CMAI, and brexpiprazole shows agitation in AD is a tractable indication, which supports a moderate prior. Against that, AD agitation trials have high and variable placebo responses, ADVANCE-1's effect was modest, and the 5-week duration leaves little time for separation, so a replication is roughly a coin flip. From memory, topline results reported in late 2024 showed ADVANCE-2 missed statistical significance on the CMAI primary endpoint, though this forecast reflects the pre-readout view.

In phase 2b, TAK-861 (oveporexton), an orexin-2 receptor agonist that directly targets the orexin deficit behind NT1, improved MWT sleep latency by roughly 20+ minutes over placebo, with large ESS gains as well. Even at about 50 patients per arm, an effect that size gives near-certain power against placebo on MWT. I recall Takeda announcing in mid-2025 that both phase 3 trials (FirstLight and RadiantLight; this record appears to be RadiantLight) met all primary and secondary endpoints. Even before the readout the forecast would have been very high, given the mechanism and phase 2 effect sizes.

The primary endpoint is operational: respiratory therapist minutes per day spent delivering active drug. Once-daily revefenacin versus ipratropium every 6 hours should mechanically favor revefenacin, if only the active doses are counted rather than the blinding saline nebulizations. That makes a significant difference plausible even with only about 21 patients, enrollment that suggests early termination. The main risks are that matched saline dosing equalizes bedside time, or that the small, early-stopped trial reports only descriptive statistics with no significant prespecified comparison.

IL-6 blockade has supporting evidence in TED: a small randomized trial of tocilizumab showed clear benefit on clinical activity, though proptosis gains were more modest. The primary endpoint is a ≥2 mm proptosis response in active TED versus placebo. Placebo response rates on this endpoint are typically 10–20%, so a moderate IL-6 effect of around 35–50% responders should reach significance with roughly 100+ active-TED participants. Uncertainty remains because IL-6 inhibition may affect inflammation more than proptosis and the trial is modest in size, so I put it somewhat above the Phase 3 base rate.

PF-06823859 (dazukibart, anti-IFN-β) strongly suppressed the type I IFN gene signature in skin in earlier studies, so the pharmacodynamic primary endpoint is mechanistically favorable. However, the trial enrolled only 8 of a planned 48 participants, and the outcome descriptions indicate just 2 placebo patients, so it was clearly terminated early. With roughly 6 versus 2 patients, a formal statistically significant comparison is unlikely to have been run or achieved, and Pfizer probably reported descriptive results only. I therefore put the chance of a formally met primary endpoint low, leaving some room for a large PD effect producing a nominal p<0.05.

MET097 is a GLP-1 receptor agonist, a mechanism that reliably produces large, significant placebo-adjusted weight loss within 28 weeks. With roughly 239 participants across four doses versus placebo, the study has ample power for percent weight change. Placebo-controlled GLP-1 obesity trials almost never miss this endpoint, and earlier Phase 1 data already showed meaningful weight loss. I recall Metsera reporting a statistically significant primary endpoint, with placebo-adjusted weight loss of up to about 14% at week 28.

SM04554 (dalosirvat) is a first-in-class topical Wnt-pathway modulator from Samumed/Biosplice. Its earlier phase 2 data on hair counts were modest and promoted mainly through company presentations rather than robust vehicle-controlled significance. This exploratory biopsy study puts about 16 subjects in each of three arms, and biopsy follicle counts are noisy, so a statistically significant difference versus vehicle on terminal follicle count at day 91 is unlikely. The sponsor's history of selective, upbeat reporting adds uncertainty, but I don't recall a clear significant result, so I lean below 50%.

Phase 3 SLE trials on SRI-4 fail often, as with rituximab in EXPLORER and several anifrolumab and atacicept programs, so the base rate is below 50%. Obinutuzumab gives deeper B-cell depletion than rituximab, and the NOBILITY and REGENCY lupus nephritis trials were positive. Enrolling only serologically active patients (low complement, positive autoantibodies) enriches for B-cell-driven disease, which should favor this mechanism. I believe Roche announced that ALLEGORY met its SRI-4 primary endpoint, but my pre-readout estimate, weighing mechanistic support against the SLE base rate and a modest sample of about 300, would be moderately above even.

This appears to be VEGA-3, a Phase 3 trial of phentolamine 0.75% monotherapy, an alpha-antagonist pupil modulator, for presbyopia. Prior VEGA-1 Phase 2 data and VEGA-2 Phase 3 data supported a modest but real near-vision benefit from pupil miosis. The sample is large and the comparator is vehicle, though a 15-letter responder endpoint at 12 hours post-dose is a demanding bar for a mild miotic. I recall Opus announcing positive topline results, but my pre-readout estimate would have been about 0.7–0.75.

Verekitug blocks the TSLP receptor, and TSLP blockade with tezepelumab has already produced large, highly significant reductions in nasal polyp score in CRSwNP (WAYPOINT), so the mechanism has strong supporting evidence. Biologics in CRSwNP typically beat placebo on NPS by about 1–2 points, with SDs around 1.5–2, so 81 participants gives high power even if the effect is somewhat smaller. The main risks are the less-frequent 12-week dosing and a small sample, but the base rate for this endpoint and mechanism is high. I believe Upstream Bio reported a statistically significant NPS improvement in VIBRANT, though my estimate rests mainly on the prior evidence.

The first primary endpoint, FEV1 AUC over 0–30 minutes after the first dose, targets onset of action. Formoterol's faster bronchodilation than salmeterol is well established, so the endpoint is designed to favour Foster. With about 210 patients per arm, a fast-onset difference over the first 30 minutes should be readily detectable. I vaguely recall the published Chiesi study (Singh et al.) reporting superior early FEV1 with BDP/formoterol and equivalent TDI, consistent with the strong mechanistic prior.

Phase 2 data (ACE-536-MF-001 cohort 3B) showed about 20–27% RBC-TI in transfusion-dependent MF patients on ruxolitinib, and luspatercept's anemia efficacy is proven in MDS and beta-thalassemia, which supports a reasonable prior. Against that, 12-week transfusion independence is a strict endpoint in heavily transfused MF patients. Placebo responses near 10% are plausible, and with about 313 patients randomized 2:1, a modest absolute difference of roughly 10 points could fall short of significance. I recall the INDEPENDENCE trial narrowly missed its primary endpoint (about 15% vs 8%, p≈0.05), but a pre-readout estimate would have been slightly better than even.

This is CCTG BR.31, adjuvant durvalumab versus placebo after complete resection of stage IB–IIIA NSCLC, with the primary endpoint being DFS in PD-L1 TC ≥25%, EGFR/ALK-negative patients. Supporting evidence is reasonable: IMpower010 (atezolizumab) and PEARLS/KEYNOTE-091 (pembrolizumab) showed adjuvant PD-(L)1 DFS benefits, and PACIFIC validated durvalumab in stage III disease. Against that, IMpower010 and PEARLS gave inconsistent results in PD-L1-high subgroups, this trial includes stage IB patients, and the very long accrual and follow-up suggest a diluted effect, so I'd put the prior near a coin flip. I recall that BR.31 was reported as not meeting its primary DFS endpoint, but my pre-readout estimate would have been about 0.45.

This is CAPItello-281. The mechanism has supporting evidence: ipatasertib plus abiraterone in IPATential150 met rPFS in the PTEN-loss subgroup of mCRPC (HR ~0.77), though the effect was modest and not considered clinically compelling. Here the trial enrols only PTEN-deficient patients, has about 1000 participants and an investigator-assessed rPFS endpoint, so it is well powered for a modest hazard ratio, though capivasertib toxicity and dose interruptions could dilute the effect. I recall AstraZeneca announcing in late 2024 that the trial met its rPFS primary endpoint; my pre-readout estimate would have been around 0.6.

Platinum-resistant ovarian cancer phase 3 trials have a poor historical success rate, and glucocorticoid receptor antagonism to restore chemosensitivity is a novel mechanism. However, a randomized phase 2 trial of the same intermittent relacorilant plus nab-paclitaxel regimen against nab-paclitaxel alone showed meaningful PFS (HR ~0.66) and OS benefit, and ROSELLA closely replicates that design with BICR-assessed PFS as the first primary endpoint. With about 380 patients, the trial has reasonable power for an HR near 0.7, so I would have put the pre-readout probability somewhat above even. I recall that Corcept announced in early 2025 that ROSELLA met its PFS primary endpoint (HR ~0.70).

Phase 2 data showed orforglipron lowering HbA1c by about 2%, at least as much as oral semaglutide 14 mg has achieved. The primary endpoint only requires non-inferiority on HbA1c, a sensitive and well-powered endpoint with about 1,700 participants, so the bar is low. Open-label dropout and tolerability imbalances add some risk, but probably not enough to sink a non-inferiority test. I recall Lilly's topline report that orforglipron met non-inferiority and also showed superiority over oral semaglutide, but my pre-readout estimate would still have been high, around 0.93–0.95.

ATX101 is an extended-release bupivacaine implant, and Allay's earlier TKA Phase 2 work reportedly showed signals of prolonged pain reduction, so this Phase 2b is a confirmatory step. Comparing against saline placebo over a 0 to 8 day AUC is a relatively favorable setup, since long-acting local anesthetics such as HTX-011 and Exparel have generally beaten placebo in TKA. Against that, TKA pain trials are noisy: spinal anesthesia and multimodal rescue analgesia compress differences, and with about 226 patients across three arms the placebo comparison may only have moderate power. Weighing these, I place the chance of success modestly above the Phase 2 base rate.

This is an investigator-initiated, open-label trial of about 210 pediatric heart transplant recipients testing superiority on a composite ordinal burden score (MATE-3) over 30 months. Events are low-frequency in this population, and adult everolimus trials showed mixed results, with benefits on CAV and renal function offset by more rejection and discontinuations, so a significant superiority win is a high bar. I recall the TEAMMATE results showed no significant difference in MATE-3 between everolimus/low-dose tacrolimus and tacrolimus/MMF, with more adverse-event-driven discontinuations in the everolimus arm. My pre-readout estimate would have been roughly 15–20%.

TYK2 inhibition is a validated mechanism in psoriasis: deucravacitinib was approved after large PASI-75 gains over placebo, and placebo PASI-75 response at week 16 is typically below 10%. With about 44 patients per arm and several doses including high BID regimens, even a modest effect from one dose would likely reach significance. The main risk is weak exposure or potency for this allosteric molecule. I recall Ventyx reporting that the primary endpoint was met but the effect size fell short of internal targets, leading to discontinuation in psoriasis.

This is a small (n=100), single-center VA phase 2 proof-of-concept trial testing whether hydroxychloroquine reduces carotid plaque volume over 18 months in CKD, an endpoint that changes slowly and is hard to move with anti-inflammatory therapy. Evidence for HCQ comes mainly from animal and observational data, and similar plaque-imaging trials of anti-inflammatories (e.g., methotrexate, losmapimod) have generally been negative. The trial started in late 2018, so COVID-era disruptions, plus the dropout typical of an older CKD population on serial MRI, likely reduced enrollment and power further. Taken together, the chance of a statistically significant primary result is low.

Setmelanotide is an approved MC4R agonist with strong efficacy in biallelic POMC/PCSK1/LEPR deficiency, and Phase 2 basket data in heterozygous carriers and SRC1/SH2B1 variant carriers showed modest but real BMI reductions. Here, though, effects in heterozygous and variant carriers are likely much smaller than in biallelic patients, and 52-week placebo-controlled sub-studies of roughly 70 participants each have limited power against a placebo arm with some weight loss. Four independent sub-studies give several chances for at least one arm to reach significance, and the endpoint is objective. I don't reliably recall the topline result, so I put the probability moderately above even.

Endothelin antagonism for portal hypertension has a plausible rationale, and adding an SGLT2 inhibitor is meant to offset ERA-related fluid retention, but HVPG-lowering phase 2 programs outside non-selective beta-blockers and statins have usually failed. The first-listed primary endpoint is Part A, a small 6-week comparison in compensated Child-Pugh A patients without a required HVPG >10 mmHg, which limits both the achievable effect and statistical power. Total enrollment of 205 looks modest for the five-arm Part B, possibly indicating an early stop. I do not clearly recall the outcome, so I sit somewhat below the phase 2 base rate.

Rocatinlimab, an anti-OX40 antibody, showed clear dose-dependent efficacy in its Phase 2b trial, and the monotherapy Phase 3 trials (ROCKET-HORIZON, ROCKET-IGNITE) met their rIGA and EASI-75 co-primary endpoints, though with modest absolute effect sizes. Adding TCS/TCI raises the placebo response and narrows the treatment difference, but with about 746 patients across two active doses there is ample power for a statistically significant difference at Week 24. I recall Amgen reporting that ROCKET-SHUTTLE met its co-primary and key secondary endpoints; setting that aside, I would still have forecast a high probability of success.

By design, the COLP arm replaces part of the oxycodone with placebo on days 4-6, roughly halving the scheduled dose, so lower MME is close to built in unless rescue medication offsets it. The main risks are the small sample (20 enrolled versus 60 planned), large between-patient variation in opioid dose, and the chance that this pilot reports no formal significance test. I vaguely recall a Spaulding pilot of conditioning open-label placebo (Morales-Quezada et al., around 2020) reporting lower opioid consumption with similar pain control. That recollection is uncertain, so I put the probability moderately above even.

PTSD pharmacotherapy trials have a high failure rate, especially small single-site Phase 2 studies of repurposed agents, and pregnenolone's only clinical support is small pilot work in schizophrenia, bipolar depression and pain, none of it in PTSD. With about 97 participants, a placebo lead-in and a strong placebo response on the CAPS-5, the trial is powered only for a moderate-to-large effect, which is unlikely for this agent. The mid-trial loosening of the inclusion criteria suggests enrollment trouble, and the inclusion of a lower-severity population would further shrink the detectable effect.

Liraglutide 3.0 mg has already shown a significant BMI effect in adolescents (SCALE Teens, about a 4.6-point placebo-adjusted difference in BMI SDS-related measures) and in adults, so the mechanism is well validated, and a placebo comparator with BMI change as the endpoint makes efficacy likely. The main risk is the small sample (n=82) and possible tolerability-driven dropouts in young children, but GLP-1 agonist effects tend to be large relative to variability. I recall that SCALE Kids (NEJM 2024) reported a -5.8% versus +1.6% change in BMI (p<0.001), but I would have forecast high success beforehand anyway.

This is APPLAUSE-IgAN. The first-listed primary endpoint is the 9-month UPCR ratio at the interim analysis, and I recall that it showed a roughly 38% proteinuria reduction versus placebo (p<0.0001), which supported accelerated approval in 2024. Before the readout, the phase 2 data already showed a dose-dependent UPCR reduction with the 200 mg dose, and proteinuria endpoints in IgAN (Nefecon, sparsentan, atrasentan) have reliably been met with samples of this size. Complement alternative pathway inhibition has a strong mechanistic rationale, and a 9-month proteinuria endpoint against placebo is a relatively easy bar, so I would have put the pre-readout probability at roughly 85-90%.

Semaglutide 2.4 mg has produced large, highly significant placebo-adjusted weight loss across the STEP program, and the earlier BARI-OPTIMISE trial showed liraglutide works after bariatric surgery, so the mechanism is well supported in this population. Even with only 70 patients, an expected placebo-adjusted difference of roughly 10% or more over 68 weeks against an SD of about 7–8% gives very high power. The main risks are dropout and single-site execution at a small scale, but these are unlikely to overturn an effect this large. I recall the trial reported a substantial, significant advantage for semaglutide, but the pre-readout estimate would already have been very high.

This is NRG-GU002. Adding docetaxel to RT plus ADT has mostly failed in localized and salvage prostate cancer (RTOG 0521 was marginal; GETUG-12 and SPCG-13 were largely negative), so the prior for a freedom-from-progression benefit is weak. Enrollment of only 175 suggests the trial stopped after the phase II portion and never moved to the phase III metastasis-free survival endpoint, which points to a failure to show benefit. I also recall the readout showing no significant improvement in freedom from progression with docetaxel.

This appears to be SCORPIO-HR, and I recall that ensitrelvir did not significantly shorten time to sustained symptom resolution versus placebo, though it did reduce viral RNA. Judged beforehand, ensitrelvir had a strong antiviral signal and positive symptom data from the Japanese SCORPIO-SR trial, which focused on five Omicron symptoms. Against that, the strict endpoint here (all 15 symptoms fully resolved, including hard-to-move ones like fatigue and cough) and a largely vaccinated, immune Omicron-era population make symptom differences hard to detect; Paxlovid's EPIC-SR missed a similar endpoint. A forecast of about 0.3 reflects that tension.

Sotatercept has robust evidence of large PVR reductions in PAH (PULSAR, STELLAR), and this trial enrolls Cpc-PH patients with a meaningful precapillary component (PVR ≥4 WU), so a hemodynamic effect is mechanistically plausible. PVR is a sensitive, objective endpoint, and about 55 patients per arm should be enough to detect a moderate effect, though HFpEF-related PH has historically been unresponsive to PAH drugs. I recall Merck reporting that CADENCE met its primary PVR endpoint. Setting that aside, my pre-readout estimate would have been moderately favorable.

Ilofotase alfa has a weak efficacy record: STOP-AKI missed its primary endpoint, and the phase 3 REVIVAL trial in sepsis-associated AKI was stopped for futility. Pharmacological prevention of cardiac-surgery AKI has a long history of negative trials, although a continuous creatinine-ratio endpoint in ~270 patients gives somewhat more power than a binary AKI endpoint. The pre-surgery, high-risk CKD population and the two-dose regimen are reasonable choices. Even so, the mechanistic evidence is modest and the base rate is poor, so a low probability is warranted.

This is a small investigator-led randomized phase II pilot of 158 patients testing cabazitaxel against weekly paclitaxel, a strong and active comparator in first-line HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer. Taxane-versus-taxane trials rarely show PFS superiority, and this one looks underpowered for anything but a large effect. I recall the published result showing similar PFS (roughly 6.7 vs 5.8 months) without statistical significance, with less neuropathy on cabazitaxel. I'd have given a low probability beforehand anyway.

This is a small single-site translational study (Kirkwood, Pittsburgh). Its first-listed primary outcomes are descriptive biomarker readouts (LAG3 and PD1 expression by scRNAseq at baseline and week 4), with no prespecified statistical comparison between the lead-in arms. I vaguely recall the associated publication (Cillo et al.) reporting mechanistic findings and a reasonable ORR for nivolumab plus relatlimab, consistent with RELATIVITY-047, but I do not recall specific numbers. Because there is no clear hypothesis test, whether this counts as meeting the primary endpoint is ambiguous, so the forecast stays near the middle with a slight lean positive given the combination's established activity.

177Lu-PSMA-617 had already shown clear rPFS and OS benefits in PSMA-selected mCRPC (VISION) and an rPFS benefit in the pre-taxane setting (PSMAfore), so the mechanism is well validated and the trial enrolls only PSMA-positive patients. The main risk is that ARDT+ADT controls hormone-sensitive disease so well that adding radioligand therapy could yield only a small, late-emerging difference. Against that, the trial is large (~1,126 patients), uses BIRC-assessed rPFS, and has an industry sponsor with deep experience of this agent, which together favor success. I recall Novartis announcing that PSMAddition met its rPFS primary endpoint (HR about 0.72), but the pre-readout estimate given here is roughly 0.72.

Metformin for oral premalignancy has only weak, uncontrolled support: the earlier single-arm M4OC-Prevent study reported histologic responses, but spontaneous and biopsy-related regression in placebo arms of oral leukoplakia chemoprevention trials is often 20–30%. Most randomized oral chemoprevention trials (retinoids aside) have been negative. Enrollment of only 34 suggests early termination or under-accrual, leaving little power to detect a moderate difference in a binary histologic response rate. A statistically significant superiority result is therefore unlikely.

Bronchiectasis exacerbation-reduction trials have a poor track record; only DPP-1 inhibition (brensocatib) has clearly succeeded, and this disease is mainly neutrophilic, so the case for an anti-IL-33 antibody is speculative. Itepekimab's COPD results were inconsistent: AERIFY-1 succeeded and AERIFY-2 failed. With about 105 patients per arm, variable 24–52 week exposure and noisy exacerbation counts, this proof-of-concept study can only detect a large effect. I vaguely recall that Sanofi reported this trial did not meet its primary endpoint, but my forecast rests mainly on the low prior.

Favezelimab/pembrolizumab showed only modest activity in anti-PD-1-refractory cHL in the phase 1/2 study (ORR about 30%, median PFS about 9 months, single-arm). LAG-3 blockade has not reproduced its melanoma success elsewhere, and Merck's favezelimab program had a futility stop in colorectal cancer. Bendamustine or gemcitabine are reasonably active in heavily pretreated cHL, and an open-label, investigator-assessed PFS endpoint in a 203-patient phase 2 gives limited power against a modest effect. I don't firmly recall this trial's result, but I have a vague sense that Merck later scaled back favezelimab, which nudges the estimate down.

Mazisotine (LY3556050) is an SSTR4 agonist that produced a positive signal in DPNP in Lilly's earlier chronic-pain master-protocol proof-of-concept study, while failing in other pain indications. That supports some prior over the low base rate for novel analgesics in neuropathic pain. Even so, DPNP trials have high placebo responses and many phase 2 dose-ranging studies fail to reproduce early signals, and ~100 patients per arm is only modestly powered for the typical 0.5–1 point NRS effect. I vaguely recall the asset being deprioritized but am not confident, so I put the probability below even.

Oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonists at adequate doses reliably separate from placebo on percent weight change by 12 weeks, and with four active arms of roughly 33 patients each, even a modest 2-4% placebo-adjusted loss should reach significance in at least one arm. My recollection is that the FALCON topline was commercially disappointing: the weight loss was modest and Terns deprioritized the obesity program in favor of TERN-701. As I recall, though, at least one dose still showed a statistically significant placebo-adjusted reduction. Tolerability-driven dropouts and dosing problems add some uncertainty.

This is a randomized-withdrawal design: patients already controlled on somatostatin analogues either continue an octreotide depot or switch to placebo, and IGF-1 control is lost quickly off therapy. That makes the placebo response rate low and the expected difference large even with 72 patients. The same design has worked before (e.g., oral octreotide in OPTIMAL, ~58% vs 19%), and octreotide's mechanism is well proven, so the main risk is formulation or pharmacokinetic failure, which Phase 1/2 data make unlikely. I recall that the ACROINNOVA 1 trial met its primary endpoint (about 72% vs 37% responders), but my pre-readout estimate would still have been very high.

Elismetrep is a first-in-class oral TRPM8 antagonist. TRPM8 has genetic support in migraine, and the program was spun out of Kallyope into a newly funded company, which hints at an encouraging earlier signal. Still, novel acute-migraine mechanisms often fail on 2-hour pain freedom: placebo rates run around 15–20%, and roughly 86 patients per arm only detect differences of about 13–15 points. Four dose arms, any one of which can count as a win, raise the odds somewhat, so I put it slightly above a coin flip.

Low-dose atropine has strong prior evidence for slowing myopia progression (ATOM2, LAMP), and this trial is large (852 children), runs 3 years, and tests two doses against vehicle, so either dose succeeding counts. Against that, ultra-low-dose 0.01% has inconsistent efficacy in Western populations, and a responder-proportion endpoint is less sensitive than mean change. I recall that the STAR trial reported statistical significance on the primary endpoint for the 0.01% dose, which later supported EU approval. My pre-readout estimate would still have been moderately above the base rate.

The base rate for repurposed or novel host-directed COVID-19 therapies in hospitalized patients was poor, and BIO101 (20-hydroxyecdysone, MasR activator) had only preclinical support for this indication. The trial also enrolled only about 238 of a planned 310 patients, leaving it underpowered for a modest effect on a composite of respiratory failure or death. I recall that Biophytis reported roughly a 44% relative risk reduction, with nominal significance mainly in the per-protocol population, while the full-analysis-set primary comparison appears to have missed p<0.05. Before the readout I would have put success at about 15–20%.

Complement inhibition has validated precedent in geographic atrophy: pegcetacoplan's FILLY and avacincaptad's GATHER1 both cut lesion growth in phase 2 trials of similar size. But C1q, the upstream classical-pathway target here, is less validated than C3 or C5, and roughly 90 patients per arm over 12 months gives only moderate power for the 20-30% effect typical of this class. A small company running a first-in-class phase 2 adds uncertainty, so I would have put this somewhat below even. I recall that Annexon reported ARCHER did not reach statistical significance on lesion growth rate, while highlighting visual-function benefits instead.

This is KEYNOTE-522. I recall pCR improving from about 51% to about 65% (p<0.001), and later a significant EFS benefit and approval. Before the readout, I-SPY2 had shown a large pembrolizumab pCR gain in TNBC (about 22% to 60%), and KEYNOTE-173 showed high pCR rates. The trial is large and double-blind against a platinum-containing chemotherapy backbone, and pCR is a sensitive endpoint, so the prior should be well above the base rate even though carboplatin raises the control pCR.

Rocatinlimab, an OX40 antibody, met its co-primary endpoints of rIGA 0/1 and EASI-75 at week 24 in the adult Phase 3 trials (HORIZON, IGNITE, SHUTTLE). The effect was modest but clearly significant, for example rIGA 0/1 of roughly 19% versus 7% on placebo. With about 530 adolescents across two doses plus placebo, power is adequate even if the TCS combination cohort narrows the difference, and adolescents usually respond similarly to adults with AD biologics. I believe Amgen reported that ROCKET-ASTRO met its primary endpoints, but my estimate rests mainly on the consistent adult data.

This is a small (24 enrolled versus 76 planned) dose-ranging Phase 2 pediatric study with no placebo arm, and its primary endpoints are crude, descriptive healing and maintenance rates. Dexlansoprazole's efficacy in EE is well established in adults and adolescents, so high healing rates (roughly 80–90%) are likely in both arms. Under the stated definition, though, success needs a significant comparison against a control, and a 30 mg versus 60 mg comparison in about 12 children per arm is very unlikely to reach significance. The main source of uncertainty is whether descriptively high healing rates would be scored as meeting the endpoint, which keeps the probability around 0.35 rather than lower.

IL-6 inhibition reliably and profoundly lowers hs-CRP; ziltivekimab in the similar RESCUE trial cut CRP by roughly 80–90% versus placebo in CKD patients, so this pharmacodynamic endpoint is close to certain to separate. With about 35 participants per arm and an expected effect this large, the trial is heavily overpowered for the primary comparison. I recall that the TRANQUILITY topline readout in 2025 reported large, statistically significant hs-CRP reductions across doses, ahead of Novartis acquiring Tourmaline. The forecast reflects only the small residual risk of execution or analysis problems.

Astegolimab, an anti-ST2 antibody, missed its primary exacerbation endpoint in the Phase IIa COPD-ST2 trial, showing only a nonsignificant ~22% reduction. Its main support is the related anti-IL-33 class, and those signals have been inconsistent: itepekimab split across AERIFY-1 and AERIFY-2, mainly in former smokers. This Phase III enrolls current and former smokers without eosinophil enrichment, so the plausible effect is about 15%, which is marginal even with about 1,380 patients and two dose arms. I recall that this trial, ARNASA, reported a roughly 15% reduction that was not statistically significant, but the pre-readout estimate would have been about 0.35–0.4.

This open-label phase II trial compares two active antiandrogens. The hypothesis is that darolutamide, with its lower blood-brain barrier penetration, causes less cognitive decline than enzalutamide, which has mechanistic and observational support (ARAMIS/ODENZA-type data). However, the primary endpoint, percent change in each individual's maximally changed CANTAB domain, is noisy, and 111 patients (under the 132 planned) give limited power to detect a between-arm difference over 24 weeks. I do not reliably recall the topline result, and head-to-head cognitive comparisons of this size usually show numerical trends without statistical significance, so I estimate a modest probability.

AZD3427 is a long-acting relaxin analogue. The relaxin mechanism has a mixed record: serelaxin failed its outcomes trials in acute heart failure, though it does have vasodilatory hemodynamic effects. The trial enrolls Group 2 pulmonary hypertension without a minimum PVR, so many patients likely have isolated post-capillary PH and little room to reduce PVR, and about 55 patients per arm undergoing right heart catheterization gives only modest power. I vaguely recall the program being deprioritized, though I'm not certain, so I sit somewhat below the phase 2 base rate.

This open-label investigator-initiated trial planned 60 patients but enrolled only 14, roughly 7 per arm, leaving very little power on a highly variable endpoint (24-hour chest tube drainage). PCC reliably corrects INR faster than plasma, but evidence that it reduces postoperative bleeding volume in cardiac surgery is mixed and typically modest. The chance of a significant difference in chest tube output with this sample is low, and the observed difference could just as easily favor plasma.

This is STEP-HFpEF DM. Before its readout, the companion non-diabetic STEP-HFpEF trial (reported August 2023) had already shown semaglutide 2.4 mg improving KCCQ-CSS by about 7.8 points versus placebo, with large weight loss. That makes success here likely, although weight loss and the treatment effect are usually somewhat smaller in people with type 2 diabetes. With about 617 patients, power to detect a 4–6 point KCCQ difference is good, which supports a high probability; I recall that the trial met both primary endpoints (KCCQ-CSS difference of about 7.3 points).

Randomized-withdrawal relapse-prevention trials of approved antipsychotics almost always beat placebo, because stabilized responders who are switched to placebo relapse at high rates. That holds even for drugs with modest acute effect sizes, like lumateperone, which had one failed acute trial. The sample of about 590 enrolled, with a large share randomized after stabilization, gives ample power for a time-to-relapse endpoint with a broad relapse definition. I recall Intra-Cellular reporting that Study 304 met its primary endpoint with a significant delay in relapse, but the pre-readout estimate based on design and class base rates would still be high.

Atrasentan already cut proteinuria by about 36% versus placebo in the phase 3 ALIGN trial in IgAN, and endothelin antagonism has shown additive antiproteinuric effects on top of SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., zibotentan/dapagliflozin). Proteinuria responds quickly and strongly to this drug class, and a within-subject crossover comparison in 54 patients gives high power even if the SGLT2i background somewhat shrinks the effect. The main risks are carryover or dropout complicating the analysis, or a smaller incremental effect than expected, so I place success at about 90%.

This is Moderna's ConquerRSV trial. The first-listed primary outcomes are safety measures with no efficacy comparison, so the relevant test is vaccine efficacy against RSV-LRTD with ≥2 symptoms over about 36,000 participants. Prefusion F stabilized antigens were strongly validated in older adults by the concurrent GSK and Pfizer programs, Moderna's mRNA platform had proven efficacy against COVID-19, and phase 1 mRNA-1345 neutralizing titers were robust, so with this sample size even modest efficacy would reach significance. The main risk was a weak RSV season giving too few cases, though the case-driven design mitigates this. I recall the trial reported about 84% efficacy in early 2023, but my pre-readout estimate would have been roughly 0.87.

This is GAVOTTE, and I recall that Roche reported neither it nor its relapsing-MS sister trial MUSETTE showed a benefit of higher-dose ocrelizumab over the approved 600 mg dose. Setting that aside, dose-versus-dose superiority trials against an already effective active comparator rarely succeed. The 600 mg dose already depletes peripheral B cells almost completely, and the ORATORIO effect in PPMS was modest (about a 24% risk reduction). The case for higher dose rested only on exposure-response modelling, and with 769 patients the trial had limited power to detect a small incremental effect on composite progression.

IGF-1R inhibition in active TED is clinically validated: teprotumumab hit proptosis-responder endpoints in OPTIC with roughly 83% vs 10% response, and Viridian's own phase 1/2 veligrotug data showed comparable proptosis responses after only two infusions. With about 113 patients, 2:1 randomization and a large expected effect size, power on this binary endpoint is very high, so the main risks are operational rather than biological. I recall that THRIVE reported positive topline results (about 70% vs 5% proptosis response, p<0.0001), but even before the readout I would have put this near 0.95.

Adding systemic therapy to TACE in intermediate-stage HCC has supporting evidence: LAUNCH (lenvatinib plus TACE) was positive, and EMERALD-1 (durvalumab, bevacizumab and TACE) met its PFS endpoint, so a VEGF-TKI plus anti-PD-1 combination is mechanistically well supported. PFS by BICR against TACE plus placebo is a relatively achievable endpoint, and 480 patients gives ample power for a plausible hazard ratio around 0.65–0.75. The main risks are earlier failures of TKIs combined with TACE (sorafenib, brivanib, orantinib) and lenvatinib toxicity limiting dose intensity. I recall that LEAP-012 was reported as meeting its PFS primary endpoint (HR about 0.66) while OS was not yet significant, but my pre-readout estimate would have been about 0.72.

Adjunctive treatments for negative symptoms of schizophrenia have a very poor track record: roluperidone, bitopertin and many glutamatergic agents all failed, and placebo response is high. AVP-786 has no clinical evidence in this indication, and its other programs, including Alzheimer's agitation, have been mixed. A placebo run-in helps somewhat, but with roughly 136 patients the trial is powered only for a moderate effect that is implausible here. I recall that Otsuka reported this trial did not separate from placebo on the primary endpoint, consistent with a low prior.

Topical NSAID patches (diclofenac, flurbiprofen) have repeatedly beaten placebo on SPID of pain-on-movement in acute ankle sprain trials run at German sites with this model, often with large effect sizes. Esflurbiprofen plaster is already approved in Japan, with strong skin penetration and efficacy in osteoarthritis. The main risk is the small sample (n=70), which leaves the trial vulnerable if the placebo response is high or the effect is smaller than assumed. The sponsor likely sized it for the large effects seen in this model, so I put success at about 75%.
